speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: RECEPTION TO MR. BALFOUR BY THE PARLIAMENT OF CANADA.
speechtext: For the information of the House, as well as of the public, I wish to announce that Right Hon. A. J. Balfour is expected to arrive in Ottawa on Sunday. That day will be observed by him as a day of rest. On Monday at.3 o'clock it is expected that he will address the Senate and the House of Commons. The members of the Senate will 'be our guests in this chamber on that occasion. Mr. Balfour will come here in procession from Government House by way of Sussex, Wellington and Metcalfe streets. As the space in this chamber is limited and as we wish to avail ourselves of it to the utmost, it is the purpose that the House shall meet at 2 o'clock on Monday, thus affording ample time for those who occupy seats on the floor and in the gallery to be seated when Mr. Balfour addresses the Parliament at 3 o'clock. It is hoped that the arrangement carried out on the occasion of the visit of M. Viviani will be carried out on the occasion of Mr. Balfour's visit, namely, that all those occupying seats on the floor of the House shall have the privilege of being presented to our visitor.

speechtext: Hon. Sir THOMAS WHITE (Minister of Finance) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 53, respecting insurance.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This Bill is introduced for the- purpose of re-enacting the Insurance Act of 1910 and of making such changes as are necessary to remove those features of the existing Act which have been declared by a recent decision of the Privy Council to be unconstitutional. There are also contained in the Bill a few amendments of a non-contentious nature, which are, however, deemed necessary for the proper administration of the Act. Most of the latter amendments were contained in a Bill introduced in the session of 1914, but not then, nor since, proceeded with.
Will the minister explain the special provision referred to?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
By a decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Coun-

cil in 1916 it was held that two most important sections of the Insurance Act of 1910, sections 4 and 70, were ultra vires. \v ith regard to section 4, which prohibits persons and ffompanies from'carrying on the business of insurance in Canada without first obtaining a license from the Insurance Department, the Privy Council held that that section was ultra vires, but the decision does not indicate the extent to which the section is ultra vires, and consequently the validity of the entire section is so impugned that at present the department has practically lost its authority to carry out the intention of the legislation of 1910 .respecting the licensing of British and foreign insurance companies doing business in Canada. Section 70 is the section of the Act which provides for penalties.
The matter has been most carefully considered by the Insurance Department, by the Department of Justice, and also by special counsel, and the conclusion has been reached that it is necessary-and I much regret to say it-to re-enact the entire Insurance Act of 1910, in order that- the Insurance Department may have authority over such companies transacting business in Canada. I think it will be found that the judgment of the Privy Council relates more particularly to the authority which the Act purported to confer with respect to prohibiting provincially incorporated companies from doing business in Canada outside of the province in which they were incorporated, but the decision as it stands leaves the larger question in doubt except in so far as the view of the Judicial Committee can be gathered from the judgment as a whole. It is the opinion of the Department of Justice that if we re-enact the measure as now introduced, the Dominion Government will have full authority over British and foreign companies carrying on insurance business in Canada, as was intended by the legislation of 1910. There are some other amendments to the Act, hut I believe they will be of a non-contentious nature, and some of them were embraced in an amending Bill which I introduced in the session of 1914.1 am extremely reluctant to introduce this Bill at the present session, and I do so only because I believe it is in the public interest that these doubts should be cleared up and that the Act should be re-enacted so as to give the Insurance Department the authority which Parliament intended it should have over insurance companies carrying on business in Canada. ,

The minister has not
stated what are the changes in sections 4 and 70. How is it proposed to get over the judgment of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would submit that on the introduction of a Bill it is not usual to go so much into detail. I shall be very glad to do that on the second reading.

The minister has not
explained the matter at all He has pointed put the difficulties but he has not stated how this Bill proposes to get over them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thought I had so stated.
You have only stated that this is a re-enactment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This Bill will give the Dominion Government, through the Insurance Department, authority to prohibit British and foreign companies from doing business in Canada except under license from the Insurance Department. That was the intention of the legislation of 1910, and the Act has been acted on in that sense since it was passed by Parliament; but the effect of the decision of the Privy Council is, as I have stated, to impugn the validity of section 4 which applies not only to Canadian incorporated insurance companies but to British and foreign insurance companies, and this legislation is to clear up the doubt and to re-establish the authority of the Insurance Department, that is to say, of the Dominion Government over such companies as we believe we can constitutionally take power to control under this new, enactment.

The total increase from 1911 to 1914 inclusive, is 563,525 acres. Increased acreage in the year 1915 ia, I 'believe, to be accounted for very largely by the response of the farmers of the Northwest to the appeal for a greater production of food. In 1915 there was a larger crop all_ over the provinces, when wheat prices were low. In 1916 there was a big price, but the wheat was a failure in Manitoba because it was attacked by black rust, and a like condition prevailed in a large part of Saskatchewan. It was only in parts of that province that they had 
a fair crop. In Southern Alberta they were fortunate in having a very large crop and they enjoyed the benefit of greatly increased prices. These were practically the same people who about two years previously had to receive relief from this Parliament to the extent of a loan of nearly $13,000,000 because of the total failure of their crop, as a result of which they had nothing to eat. A great deal of this money was advanced for the purchase of provisions, but these people had the courage to remain there and give the country another trial, and they have received their reward. They have had two good crops since that time, and while they received a low price in 1915, they enjoyed a large price in 1916. But I would like to point out to the; House that the total average price received by the . farmers is not as great as it is believed to be by seme people. The average includes the product of the farm of Mr. Noble, who has been quoted so often as having a thousand acres in wheat producing 54 bushels to the acre and selling at $1.87 a bushel. As *I shall show later, the average price of wheat for the whole province, including that realized by Mr. Noble, is nothing like that figure.
The effect of the adoption of the amendment proposed in conjunction with a plah that I have for land settlement, and which I hope to submit to the House at the earliest opportunity, would, I believe, very much increase the population by offering greater inducements to people to settle on the land and would increase production to a large extent. But, there is one matter that I wish to speak about. We are often told that we should not complain when "we are getting $3 a bushel for our wheat, and that we hardly know what to do with our money in the West. But, I want to show that the farmers are not receiving $3 for >vheat or anything like that. In my own case, in 1915, I had a pretty large crop. I sold my oats for 26, 28 and 31 cents iby the carload. I kept my wheat over until last year, and I was very glad to get $1.23 a bushel for it. It was good wheat, too. I did not receive $3. I do not want $3 a bushel for my wheat, if it is going to force the consumer to pay $7 or $8 a bag for his flour. This great difference between the price that the farmer receives for his wheat and the price of flour is occasioned by circumstances entirely beyond the control of the farmer. I have a few comparative figures on this subject. From the Fort William price of Saskatchewan grain we have to deduct 11 cents for wheat,

7 cents for oats and 9 cents for barley, taking my own shipping point for example and the chargee are much more for points farther west.

What is the deduction
for-freight?

We pay 16 cents per hundredweight, freight, one cent per bushel for handling charges and commission. If we hold the grain over it is a cent a month for elevator charges. We averaged from 1910 to 1914, including same, 74 cents a bushel for wheat. 54 cents was the lowest and 69 was the highest outside of 1914, but in 1914 the price was $1.48. That price was occasioned by the light crop we had in the West. Including that $1.48, the average for those years was 74 cents a bushel. In 1915 it was 81 cents a bushel. That was the year of the big, high-grade crop of grain. In 1916 the price was $1.28 a bushel due to the poor yield and low grade resulting from an attack of black rust. Prices were good though, even for poor wheat. But the yields were so very small except in spots, with the exception of southern Alberta, that the farmers did not get anything like what they were Supposed to have got, and they are certainly not responsible for the increase in the price of flour to the consumer.
Oats averaged at Fort William from 1910 to 1914, 29 cents a bushel; in 1915, 28 cents a bushel, in 1916, 46 cents a bushel. Had it not been for our oat crop in Saskatchewan a good many of us would have been pretty nearly on the rocks, so far as farming is concerned.
Barley averaged, from 1910 to 1914, 38 cents a bushel; in 1915, 43 cents a bushel; in 1916, 77 cents a bushel.
Flax averaged, from 1910 to 1914, $1.09 a bushel; in 1915, $1.50 a bushel; in 1916, $2.23 a bushel. [DOT]
I am not complaining, but I want to show that there is no reason for the statement that the farmers are receiving abnormal prices for their wheat, that everything is going well and that they should not make any complaint but should be satisfied with what they are getting. I am not advancing these arguments for the sake of individual farmers, but because I believe that some changes along these lines should be made. We have the country, we have the land, and what we must do is to have the right kind of people go on the land and stay with the country. They will not do that unless it is profitable to do so. However, if this change were made it would mean that sufficient revenue could
not be collected through the custom house. The people of this country must pay the cost of running the country. The cost of running the country does not come from any other people except of Canada. They have got to pay it in any case. It "is merely a question of the method. I think that the method could be improved, that the country would go forward under a different sys- . tern, that the people would not feel the burden of taxation to the same extent as it would be equally distributed; and immigrants would no.t be deterred from coming to the country on account of that burden.
A great many of the articles that now come into this country do not yield very much revenue to the Government. They yield an enormous, revenue, however, to the manufacturers. The question is, is the country to continue paying tribute to the manufacturers? I do not think the people can afford to do both, not only pay the taxes necessary to run the country and defray the expenses of the war but also enrich the manufacturers and put them into the bulky millionaire class. We know something of their position, and we have a right to draw the conclusion that many of them, particularly the makers of agricultural implements, could do without the enormous protection which they enjoy. They are selling, and under-selling their rivals, in foreign markets. Surely if they can under-sell their competitors in foreign countries they can do so in this country!
I have already said that there is one feature of this resolution that I should like to have altered, and no doubt if it were adopted it would be altered; that is that there should be a provision that the manufacturers should get their raw material free if they were required to lose their protection on the finished articles. The best alternative would be direct taxation in some form or other. Under the customs system, the duty is paid by the consumer. If the importer, in the first place, pays the duty on a foreign-made article, he passes that charge on to the wholesaler and he to the retailer; the retailer passes it on to his customer, and it is ultimately paid across the counter. Many of the people hardly know that they are being taxed. At the same time they are taxed very heavily. If the goods are not made across the line or in some other foreign country, the wholesaler pays the tribute to the manufacturer and it is eventually passed on, in the same way, to the consumer. Therefore, the consumer is paying not only the taxes to keep up the Government institutions and bear the bur-

dens that we all expect to bear but also immense sums in tribute to the local manufacturers.
I have been accused of being the first member to propose direct taxation in this House, in connection with the Budget speech two years ago when the Minister of Finance introduced his so-called war tax of 7i per cent. Whether that is so or not, I certainly believe it is the proper and only fair method of collecting taxes to run this country. It is the principle that is followed by financial institutions and is the business method; and I do not see why the whole country of Canada cannot be administered along common sense lines. If the population increases, as I believe it will if proper inducements are held out to them, we would not only have more people but a more prosperous people to bear all these burdens; and there is no doubt that they would bear them willingly and without complaint as long as they knew they were only paying their share.
Referring to the income tax, I have heard it suggested that men receiving under $4,000 should be exempted from income tax. I think that any man who is earning any money at all, whether he is earning $2,000 or $4,000, is paying a heavy tax under present conditions. I do not see why any man should be exempted from income tax; he is a citizen of the country, no matter what his income may be. But the tax should be proportionate. Under such a system as I propose, every man would be relieved of a great many burdens, and probably a dollar earned under this system would be equal to one dollar and twenty-five cents with our present system of protective duties, and a man could then well afford to pay, say, five cents or so directly out of each dollar of his income towards keeping up the institutions of the country. As a citizen I think every man has a duty to do so, unless you come down to the very poor who are practically, to some extent, subsisting on charity. Under present conditions, every man who buys anything to-day is paying either a tax to the Government indirectly or a tribute to the manufacturer, and if he is relieved of these imposts he can well afford to pay a small portion of his income towards keeping up the institutions of the country. I feel that this is a very important matter indeed. I am not talking simply because I happen to be a farmer from the West, but I am looking at it from the standpoint of the necessities of the country and the welfare of the whole empire. I believe that, notwith-
[ Mr. MacNutt.]
standing the arguments advanced against it which we have heard before, although they have not impressed me as being very good arguments, the best and proper method of obtaining funds from the people of Canada to keep up our public institutions, pay off our public debts, and so on, and to develop the country, would be to levy direct taxes of some kind that would be proportionate according to the ability of each citizen to pay. Feeling this way, I have no hesitation in saying that I will support this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I am aware of the fact thjt a discussion on the tariff is, perhaps, not as interesting as other discussions which the House will listen to in the near future, but I have no apology to make for taking up a few moments of the time of the House in supporting the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). Some of the domestic problems which press upon our attention are, perhaps, as important as the furnishing of additional troops for service at the front. This great war has added new and very heavy responsibilities to Parliament and to this country, particularly by reason pf the enormous debt that has been created and that will be created before and after the conclusion of the war. These responsibilities must be bravely met and squarely faced by the people, .and it is not with any desire to make a special plea for the lightening of the lawful burdens of any section pf the people that I give my support to an amendment which calls for a reduction of duties along certain lines. But Canada's present and future responsibilities must be met in a fair and equitable way; the burden of taxation should not press unduly upon any particular class pf our population. The basic industries of Canada-mining, the development of our forests and fisheries, and so on-will have to produce the wealth necessary to meet the enormous obligations resting upon this country now and *which will rest upon it in the future. Only by the development of her basic industries will Canada be able properly to bear the burden of meeting these obligations. I shall confine my remarks more particularly to the one great industry of Canada, agriculture.
In normal times agriculture is regarded as an occupation not as attractive as many others. Even in times of peace, one of the great difficulties of this country, which is so admirably suited to agriculture, is to get our young men to stay on the farm rather

than go to the crowded town or city. That condition will be accentuated after the war is over. The soldier who 'has become accustomed to community life in his experience overseas will not be easily induced to go upon the land. 'The only remedy for this condition is to make farm life so attractive that not only the people at home, but many of our soldiers after their return from overseas, may be induced to go upon the land and thus increase the production of natural wealth which is so necessary to enable us to meet our responsibilities.
Two or three things are essential to make farm life attractive. I may be uttering platitudes when I speak about these things, but it is necessary that they be
4 p.m. emphasized again and again.
First, if we wish to make agri-. culture an attractive occupation for the young men of our country, both those at home and those now overseas, we must make it profitable. That, after all, is the one great thing. In nprmal times the acquiring of great wealth on the farm is the rare exception. The farmer who succeeds in meeting the ordinary obligations of life and in giving his family an education and a fair start in life is counted as a very successful man, from the standpoint of the agriculturist. These suggestions are not made with a view to having the farmer become a member of the millionaire class. Speaking more particularly for the newer parts of Canada, I can say that the average farmer finds his hands full in endeavouring to make both ends meet-and in a great many cases he is unable to do even that.
If farming is to be made more profitable than it is at present there are two or three things that must be done. In the first place, it is the duty of this Government and of this Parliament to see that the cost of production is made as low as possible. The second section of the amendment deals with that when it says:-
2. That farm implements and machinery, farm tractors, mining-, flour and saw-mill machinery, and repairs for same, rough and partly dressed lumber, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils, cement and fertilizers be added to the free list.
jMo one can fairly say that it is just that the farmers, in the matter of the cost of production, should be placed at a disadvantage in comparison with the farmers of the great republic to the south. We know perfectly well, however, that they are placed at such a disadvantage in that they have to pay very much higher prices for the tools, so to speak, of their trade, and that is the
direct result of the tariff imposed upon farm machinery coming into this country. The farmer of any part of Canada, when he advocates that farm machinery be placed upon the free list, does not thereby exclude himself from the list of the taxpayers of this country, because the farmer wears clothing, boots and shoes; he buys furniture for his house and harness for his horses, and on all of those things he must pay a tax, because, whether they are manufactured in Canada or in other countries, the tariff increases the cost to -the purchaser. Therefore, like the rest o.f us, the farmer, even if farm machinery be put on the free list, will continue to contribute his fair share towards the maintenance of the revenues of the country. But when you come to tax the tools of the farmer's trade, that is to say, to put a heavy tax on farm machinery, then you are doing an injury, not to the farmer alone, but to the whole country, in that you are discouraging men from engaging in an occupation which we all believe to be, after all, the foundation of the future greatness and wealth of this country of ours.
We must cheapen the cost of production; we must also furnish the farmer with wider markets for the products of his farm, and in this connection I must express my very great pleasure at the action that has been taken by the Government in placing wheat and wheat flour on the free list. That has been done as a war measure, it is true, but nevertheless we believe the measure will be a permanent one, because I am sure that once the farmers of the country have enjoyed the benefits of wider markets, they will never willingly give them up, and there will be a very strong protest if any attempt is made in the future by any political party to take away this privilege. It is questionable how much direct benefit will accrue in the near future to the farmers of the country from that action, but even at the present time I am sure that the western farmer who had last year a very considerable quantity of the lower grades of wheat in his granary or in the elevators awaiting sale, will find that he has derived very great benefit The permanency of this measure is one upon which I would very much like to insist. Wheat and wheat flour have been, as I have said, put upon the free list by Order in Council as a war measure, and I am happy to say that so far no great harm has resulted to other industries in this country from the Government's action in this respect. It is true there was a little flurry amongst the millers who made some slight protest to the Government in con-

nection with'its action in this matter, but I am sure there is no question in the mind of any member in this House that any real or lasting injury has been done to the milling industry of this country by the placing of wheat and wheat flour on the free list. In any case, it is surely true that the man who grows the wheat should be the man fited by having free markets for wheat or kind, and it is the most idle thing to argue in this House the question as to whether or not the western farmer would be bene-fitted by having free markets for wheat or wheat products, when the western farmer himself is fully convinced that he would so 'benefit. Surely he is the best judge, and surely if he says that he fears no competition from the wheat producers of any other country and that all he requires is reciprocity in the matter of the products of his farm, his judgment, as a man watching the markets of the world and knowing the value of his product, should take precedence over that of any other person, and his decision in the matter should be final so far as this Government, this Parliament' and this country is concerned.
Another reaeon why I am glad to see the action taken by this Government in this matter is that, in my judgment, the placing of wheat and wheat flour on the free list is going to assist very materially in removing that situation that has in times past arisen not once but many times so far as the transportation of our farm products is concerned; that is to say, if the farmer is to get the best result from his toil, he must be able to market his product at the time most suitable to his own convenience. In the past that has not been the case; the farmer has had to suit hie convenience to that of the transportation companies. We have a congested condition of traffic that means that the farmer who is ready to market his crop in a slack season of the year is not able to do so and has to wait sometimes for weeks and even months by reason of that transportation congestion. Now that wheat and wheat flour have been placed on the free list, that condition will be enormously relieved, in that, if the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur, the Government interior elevators and the private elevators elsewhere throughout the country are congested,
I trust that we shall never again see that anomaly of our freight cars, not a few but hundreds and hundreds of them, that have brought settlers and their effects-into western Canada during the early months of the

year, going back to the United States without a single pound of freight. That has happened time and again in this country, and it was most aggravating to the farmers whcr were crying out for transportation facilities to see empty cars going across the International boundary simply because of the tariff on farm products. But fortunately, the congestion can never become so acute in the future by reason of the placing of wheat and wheat flour on the free list. The storage facilities of the great milling interests to the south will be available, and our railways running from western Canada into the United States will he able to relieve the congestion that hitherto has prevented our farmers from marketing their grain at the proper time.
The farmer is not averse to paying his fair share of the revenue of this country, but we all know very well that a protective tariff is not an equitable way of obtaining revenue. Something may be said perhaps in favour of .a tariff based on revenue necessities, but no just argument can be made in favour of a protective tariff, because under a protective tariff a large part of the extra taxation that is borne by the people does not go into the treasury, but into the pockets of the interests receiving that protection. It will, however, he the policy of this country probably for many years to come to maintain a tariff for revenue purposes; probably we cannot get away from that. But a tariff for revenue, as I understand it, means the difference between the cost of production on the south of the line as compared with the cost of production of the same article on this side of the line. . When you go beyond that, you are protecting an interest; it is not the public or the treasury that gets the benefit, but simply and solely the protected interests.
Clause 3 otf the amendment of the hon. member for Edmonton, which seeks to have staple foods and food products, etc., come into Canada free of duty, touches a question that is vital to the hearts and minds of the people of this country at the present time. Coming back to this country only a few months ago from overseas, where the people are supposed to be on the brink of a food shortage, and where prices are considered extraordinarily high, it was a very great shock to me to find how high the prices of food products had gone in this country, which is supposed to he a country of production above anything else. It is a marvel how many thousands of people in this country are able to exist to-day in view of the prices they have to pay for every single

article of food that goes on their table. If a wounded soldier returns to Canada, and is classed as 100 per cent incapacitated, he gets a pension of $480 a year. He is unfit to earn a living, and is supposed to keep himself and his family on that $480. Just think of the prices he has to pay right here in the city of Ottawa for everything he puts on his table: 50 cents a pound for butter, 50 cents a dozen for eggs, $4 to $4.50 a bag for potatoes, and so on. In view of these prices, does any one think that a returned soldier, out of business so far as earning his own livelihood is concerned, can live actually live on $480 a year? What is the reason for these high prices? Are prices high because there are no eggs or potatoes in this country? Are we paying 50 cents a pound for butter because no butter is to he found in this Canada of ours? Is the extraordinarily high price of meat due to a scarcity of domestic animals in this country? I have not had occasion to visit any of the cold storage plants in this country, but I imagine if one were to make a tour of inspection of them he would soon discover that there was no very great shortage of the food that the people require for their table. The fact is-I think we all know it; it is a conviction in the minds of the people, at any rate-that the men who deal in food products in this country are storing up food products, using the war as an excuse for so doing, in order that they may charge high and yet higher prices. Somebody may say: You advocated high prices for wheat, you want the farmer to get a good price, yet you complain about the high price of flour. Yes, there might be some contradiction there, if there were any equitable ratio between the increased price of flour and the increased price of wheat, but we know perfectly well that there is not. We know that if wheat is selling on the exchange at $3 a bushel, that is by no means the price the farmer gets for it; it i3 not the price the millers of Canada paid for the millions of 'bushels they now have in storage in their elevators throughout this country. But immediately the price of wheat jumps on the exchange up goes the price of flour, although the miller who is boosting the price of flour has in his possession at that very time wheat that cost him, not $3 a bushel, but perhaps not more than half that amount. If the price of wheat on the exchange were to drop from $3 to $2 to-morrow we know perfectly well there would be no such corresponding drop in the price of flour. '	.
It has never been so; it is not so now. Something has to be done to meet the situaiio	i w

These people are getting high prices for their-labour and consequently are able to bear the present high cost of living. But I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what about the soldier's dependents? We know what the pay of the ordinary soldier is-it is $1.10 a day. If he assigns half his pay, that much goes to his family, and they also get $20 a month of separation allowance from the Government and then a -much smaller contribution from the Patriotic Fund. But add all these together, and consider xhe case of a soldier's wife with several children living in this city, or in Montreal, or in Toronto, or in Winnipeg. Ask yourself how are our soldiers' families actually living, or existing, in view of what they have pay for rent, for clothing, for food, and for everything else.
It is to be presumed that, unless something very radical is done, the cost of living will not be lower than at present, and may be greatly increased. But, immediately the war is over, there is going to be a great re-adjustment of industrial conditions. Munition factories will be closed, and their highly-paid workers will have to seek other employment. Wages are going to drop more to the normal level of the times before the war, but the cost of living will remain high for some time to come. Is ' not this a vital question, to be considered right now by the Government, and the Parliament, and the people of this country? I say quite frankly that I have very little faith in legislation or legislators as a means of breaking up these food combines that, we believe, now exist. There is only one way in which they can be broken up, and that is by competition, by allowing food products, as the amendment says, to come into Oanada free of duty. .

The hon. member has
dwelt especially on the prices of flour. He also says that to allow the free entry of goods will reduce the prices of those goods. Flour is now on the free list, yet the hon. gentleman complains of the high prices. How does he propose to deal with this particular evil?

must be remembered also that since this change was made the United States of America have gone into the war, and similar conditions prevail over there to those that prevail here with regard to the price of flour. But I am speaking not only of war time but of the time to come when we shall tend again towards normal conditions. Placing wheat flour on the free list will, in my opinion, have great effect in reducing the price. For my hon. friend from Muskoka (Mr. Wright) knows very well that the people of Canada in pre-war times paid more for their flour than did the people of the adjoining states of the Republic.
I do not know that.

I am satisfied I am correct in that assertion. But wheat flour is not the only item. How about eggs, butter, meat and other products? We have other countries to draw upon for these things, which countries, at present, like ourselves, are engaged in war; but I confidently assert that the free exchange of food products between Canada and these other countries as indicated in the amendment, will have the effect of breaking up food combines in this country.
But, even assuming that I do not offer the right remedy, yet we must admit that we are face to face with a condition that must be dealt with. We are not going to pension our returned soldier at $480 a year and expect him to pay present prices for all that he has to buy. If the Government by legislation can effect a remedy, it is time the Government were taking the necessary steps to that end. For, as we see it, conditions are not improving, but are rapidly growing worse in this regard.
I support the last clause of this amendment also, but in a less whole-hearted way than I support the clauses which precede it. This last clause deals with the British preference, and the proposal of the hon. member for Edmonton is that this preference shall be increased to fifty per cent of the tariff. This principle of preference to imports from Great Britain is one which this House adopted years ago, but the fixing of the rate at the definite figure of fifty per cent is necessarily somewhat arbitrary. I presume, however, that if we are to deal with the subject at all, some figure must be agreed upon. Perhaps this is a subject that might very well be considered to greater advantage in the days to come, when the trade relations between the dif-
	,
ferent parts of the Empire will undoubtedly form one of the great questions to be considered by the statesmen of Canada, the other self-governing dominions and the Mother Country. So far as this particular part of the amendment is concerned, while I give my support to it, I do it with that idea in mind-that, if the principle is to be maintained, perhaps this particular percentage is not too great a preference to give to goods coming into Canada from Great Britain.
In conceding my remarks, I febl that every one in this House is seized of the important problems that present themselves for our consideration at the present time and the very great responsibility that rests upon the Government of this country. Government, in ordinary times, is not the easiest thing in a democratic country where free discussion is the order of the day. Anything I have said to-day has not been in the spirit of adverse criticism of the Government but simply to call attention to certain conditions that actually exist and to urge upon the Government and Parliament the necessity of taking action in dealing with the same. I know that the farmer of western Canada does not get very much sympathy these days because of the comparatively high price that he is getting for his products. But, Sir, I have seen the same farmer in the lean years gone by when he should have had a good deal more consideration than he actually got from this Government and this Parliament. It i3 in view, not merely of present conditions, that I support this amendment, but the conditions to be provided for, of the conditions of the future. The Government are proposing some new legislation to deal with the question of the returned soldier and to provide for placing him on our western Canadian .land; I presume that is where they intend to put him because they have not any land anywhere else and they are going to take ours in the western provinces. Under the very best of conditions and circumstances, they will find great difficulty in carrying out this project. Under the very best of conditions, as they have been in the past, we have found it very difficult. We have had to spend great sums of money to get people from other countries to come and settle on our splendid agricultural land. We have had to give a free bonus of 160 acres of the finest agricultural land lying out of doors anywhere. These conditions are rapidly passing away. We have not the free homesteads in the same abundance that we had

in former days. The best of them have been taken up. You cannot go to Manitoba, Saskatchewan, or Alberta, and find first class homesteads nearer than 10 to 15 miles of the railway. You have to go beyond that if you want to secure Government * land for future homestead settlement. These are the conditions that you are face to face with. I will venture .to prophesy, and I am neither a prophet nor the son of a prophet, that the Government land settlement scheme for soldiers will absolutely fail unless the Government undertake to make farming conditions a great deal more attractive in our western provinces than they are at the present time. We hope to attract an increased population to Canada after the war for the purpose of settling on our agricultural lands in the West and for the purpose of increasing agricultural production so that we may be in a position to meet our enormous war bills. But, I venture to say that we will have an insurmountable, an impossible, task on our hands if we hope to secure that immigration or settlement and allow tariff and transportation conditions to remain as they are at' the present time in this country. For that reason, and in order that the agricultural and other natural resources may be developed, in order that our returned soldiers may be induced to go on the farms, in order that a first class immigration may be attracted to this country and in order that Canada's future may be assured, I am here to-day to support, and I am prepared to vote for, the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Edmonton.

What is the situation in regard to international boundary surveys now?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The international boundary surveys are drawing to a close. There is yet some work to be done on the Ontario-Minnesota boundary, according to article V of the treaty. The field work undertaken by the British Commission on this section of the line was finished during the past season. It has been decided, however, to improve the triangulation across the lake of the Woods. This will be undertaken by the United States Commissioner, and the Canadian Commissioner will co-operate to the extent of furnishing a motor boat and three men.
Then there 'is the Quebec and Vermont State line. Though the actual demarcation was completed in 1907, it was found necessary and agreed to, between the former Commissioners, "that a controlling triangulation should be executed along the 45th parallel from Hall's stream to the St. Lawrence river, and that the country along the portion of the boundary of New York state should be mapped." This item is to pay the expenses of a survey party to be employed in the execution of such a controlling triangulation, from Hall's stream to the Richelieu river, a distance of 80 miles.

Then there is the Quebec-Maine boundary -under article III of the treaty oif 1908. This article provides for the re-survey of the boundary from the source of the St. Croix to the St. Lawrence river. This section has all been completed with the exception of a comparatively small portion of so-called high lands boundary along the eastern side oif the townships of Beauce and Frontenac.
Then there is the St. John and St. Croix rivers survey under articles III and II, for recovering, replacing and tying in of the original boundary reference marks of 1843-5 along the St. John river, and also to assist in executing certain topograph mapping, monumenting and triangulation along the St. Croix river from its source to Baring, Maine. This work along the New Bruns-wick-Maine boundary is to be undertaken by the United States Commissioner, and the Canadian Commissioner proposes sending a representative, with one man, to cooperate.

I understand that Mr. Hay has been for a few years in the employ of the Dominion Immigration Department and he has been acting in co-operation with the provincial Governments in the colonization scheme they have adopted. I have been given to understand that he has been doing very good work.

If all the other agents throughout the country to whom the minister is paying salaries, are doing the same quantity of work for the salaries they are receiving as Mr. Hay is doing, then this vote, instead of being $580,000, should be cut down to $25, because Mr. A. W. Hay is doing nothing in connection with the Dominion Government and nothing in connection with the Government of New ,Brunswick. He was on a board that was called the Farm Settlement Board. They started out with the idea of buying up abandoned farms and bringing in settlers from England, Scotland, and Ireland, but in the first year or two of the appointment of the Board, they brought in probably 30 or 40 persons of this class. Then they started to act as a land office and they used the money of the province in buying a farm from one man to sell it to another. There was also a political consideration. In the last election, to my certain knowledge, they went to men to whom they had sold farms and said to them: Now you vote right or we will drive' you off your farms because you are in arrears. I do not believe Mr. Hay has brought a single immigrant into the province of New Brunswick in the last two years. It is a surprise to me and it will be a surprise to a good many people in New Brunswick to learn that this man has been drawing, not only a salary from the Dominion Government but a salary from the Government of New Brunswick, I would like to know how much he has been drawing from the Dominion Government.

He has been drawing a
salary of $1,500 a year from the Dominion

Government. As I have said, he has been acting in co-operation with the provincial authorities. Their land settlement scheme was in its infancy about the time of the outbreak of war, and that, of course, gave it a setback as might be expected, but Mr. Hay's services have been continued by the department, although we have dismissed certain of our officials, and I am not aware that Mr. Hay has been drawing another salary from the provincial government.
Does the minister say that he is proposing to pay Mr. Hay a salary of $1,500 this year? ,
Well, we have estimated for that salary for the coming year.
In that case, I will ask this committee to divide on this proposed vote unless the minister will agree to dismiss Mr Hay summarily.

The minister does not usually dismiss a man summarily upon the dictation of a member of the Opposition without making some further inquiries, and I think the hon. member will see that it would be unfair to Mr. Hay to do so. I will inquire into the matter, and if the circumstances are as set forth by the hon. member for Oarleton, I certainly would not feel justified in retaining Mr. Hay dn the employ of the department, if he is being paid by the provincial government and is-doing no work.
He is certainly doing no work; he is drawing a salary.
If he is doing no work, I would not keep him on the pay-list, but at the same time-
Is he also receiving anything for expenses, and if so, how much?
If he has received any, it has been a very small amount.
I would like to know exactly how much, even if the amount be small.

He received nothing at all
for expenses last year.

The minister says that if the circumstances regarding Mr. Hay are as the hon. member for Carleton says, namely, that this gentleman is not doing any work, the minister will not feel disposed to,pay him a salary. Will that same remark -apply to all the other employees covered by this vote of $580,000, that i's, if the minister is convinced that any of them

are not doing any work? I do not think matters of this kind should require to be pointed out by members. Does not the minister keep in touch with his employees in order to see that they are working?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The minister does not carry on correspondence with all the 500 odd employees of the department. Those who are not at the front are doing good work, but many officials have enlisted and are still receiving salaries. A great deal of extra work that the House does not realize has been thrown upon our immigration officers by reason of the war, in the way of looking after boundary inspection in particular, and assisting the other departments in other work.
How many immigrants came into Canada last year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: A little over 75,000.

Will the minister say how many other immigration officials he has in the county of Carleton, where they are located, their names and their salaries? I ask this question for this reason: There was a time when foreign labourers were coming into the province of New Brunswick on account of railway construction, and at that time there were a few immigration agents whose salaries were justified. That, however, is all past and gone now, and I know there are, besides Mr. Hay, two or three other men employed as immigration officials, who, I think, are doing very little.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Can the hon. member give me their names?

There have been so many * political changes in that country that I have forgotten the names. There is one at Debec, I think. A man died, and I have forgotten who has been appointed in his place, but in the immediate vicinity of Mr. Hay there must be at least half a dozen other immigration officials who are receiving fair salaries but who possibly may be doing something. I quite understand there may be some justification for these others, but for Mr. Hay there is absolutely no justification whatever except to furnish a good fat salary for a very earnest political worker for the Conservative party. I do not think this country in its present condition can afford to pay salaries of $1,500 a year to friends of the political party of my hon. friend for doing nothing.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The hon. gentleman must be misinformed-
I am not misinformed.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: With the exception of Mr. Hay there is no other official in the county of Carleton in the employ of this department.
No others? I think there must be.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: My information is that in the county of Carleton there are no other paid [DOT]officials of this department.
What efforts, if any, have been made during the past year to secure immigrants from the United States? Has the minister made any trips to the United States in connection with immigration?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We have carried on a very active propaganda in the United States above all other countries. A year ago there was an active campaign in the press of the United States to prevent settlers from coming to this country. Conditions in Canada were misrepresented. It was stated that settlers who came over here would be enlisted in our army, that that was why we were anxious to get them over here, that they would 'be taxed to death by reason of the war, and that there were such heavy land taxes in the western provinces that it would he unwise for any settlers to leave the United States for Canada, particularly as certain of the states had enlarged the homestead allotments from 160 to 640 acres, though this was generally in the case of inferior land. It was, therefore, considered advisable to have a conference of all our immigration agents in the United States. They met at Chicago, and I attended personally. Before going I invited the premiers of the three western provinces to attend, and each of them were represented .at the conference. We discussed immigration matters, found out the exact nature of the propaganda that was being carried on in the United States, and determined on active steps to combat it.
What steps did you take?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We carried on an extensive publicity campaign in the press of the United States. Their papers were very fair, and many of them were willing to insert articles giving the actual facts. We .also carried on a more extensive advertising campaign than ever before, with such good results as to bring forth encomiums from the premiers of the western provinces, who personally complimented the department on the work we were doing. They realized . that the slump in immigration from the

United States was not due to any lack of interest or activity on the part of the Dominion Immigration authorities. We secured 75,000 immigrants last year, as compared with 48,000 the previous year, and of that 75,000, 61,000 came from the United States. Our campaign is still having good results, because the immigration during the present fiscal year has increased from 50' to 75 per cent, and from some of the States by 100 per cent. Considering that the war is on, I think we are getting quite a large number of immigrants from the United States.
That is the best country to obtain immigrants from at the present time?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
Will the minister state what means were adopted in the United States to prevent settlers from coming to Canada? What -steps did the minister take to reassure intending immigrants about enlistments?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman is quite aware what steps we took, because the papers were all brought down.
I do not remember. I saw statements in the newspapers.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: In January or February, 1916, I contributed a letter over my signature stating that there was no conscription in Canada, that the Government did not think it either necessary or advisable, and that even if it should be resorted to, it would not apply to American citizens. This letter was spread broadcast throughout the United States.
They would not be liable to conscription if they became British subjects?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I did not say that.
They could not take up homesteads unless they were British subjects.
Oh, ye6, but they would not be able to secure the patent. They could become British subjects before the end of the three years.
Were there any restrictions in regard to the nationality of these , settlers from the United States? Were people of enemy birth or origin admitted?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We exercised discretion in that matter. We do not allow men of German nationality to enter Canada.
What about men of German origin who have become American citizens.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We should not debar them if they were American citizens.
The suggestion has been made in this House to disfranchise those of enemy origin.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Has the Government proposed that?
I understand some -hon. gentlemen have suggested it.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I cannot help that.

The gentleman (Mr. R. B. Bennett) who made the proposal to the House is reported to have gone to the United States some months ago, as Chairman of the National Service Commission, and- to have succeeded in getting quite a large number of Americans to come over here to assist in farming operations. As the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) is not present, perhaps the minister could tell us the results of his mission.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The chairman of the National Service Commission co-operated with the provincial governments and with our department in order to meet the demand for farm labour. We knew that a very large number of farm labourers would be required, and that it would be impossible to get them in Canada. So, acting in co-operation with the provinces, we added to our staff for the time being just the same number of men as the respective provincial governments appointed; for instance, Manitoba sent six agents to the United States, and we sent an equal number; Saskatchewan sent over ten, and we sent over ten; Alberta sent over -six, and we sent over six. The campaign, I am glad to say, was successful in bringing in all the help that was desired. Between 8,000 and 9,000 men came in, and they were distributed over the different provinces through agencies appointed by -the provincial governments. We had to issue instructions some time ago recalling our men, as the provincial governments had notified us they had all the labourers they wanted.
Were these labourers Brought in temporarily, or have a number of them become settlers? '

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: A number of them have no doubt returned, hut we hope and expect that a number of them will -become permanent settlers.
Has the minister any of the literature that was distributed when that campaign was on in conjunction with the National Service?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The papers were brought down and laid on the Table, at the request of the hon. member for Pictou.
All the literature?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
My hon. friend advertised in the United States for farm hands. Have these papers been brought down?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The advertisements were. Mr. LEMIEUX: How many farm hands were got?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: In the neighbourhood of 9,000.
How were they distributed?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Alberta got approximately 3,500, Saskatchewan 4,700, and Manitoba 800.

Do I understand the
minister to say there are no restrictions as regards the nationality of these people?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Oh yes. Positive instructions were given to admit no one of enemy nationality.	-

Were there restrictions
as to people of enemy origin?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
If the person of enemy
origin had become an American citizen, we admitted him.

Were the agents that
the Dominion Government appointed for this special work regular employees of the department or new men?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Some of them were on our permanent staff. Others were nominated by the National Service Commission; they were hired for one month only.
When their work was over did they remain in the department?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.

I should like the minister to state what inducements he offered to these immigrants in the way of taking up
homesteads.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Any of these farm labourers from the United States could take up a homestead under our regular homestead laws. The only concession we granted was that the time spent as a farm labourer in Canada this year would be counted as residence upon a homestead.

Has the minister had a
table compiled showing how many of these men were of enemy origin or nationality?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We did not keep tab on that, except by judging from the names.

Has the minister had occasion to read the Duke of Connaught's farewell address to the Canadian Club, in which he said the future of Canada rested with the importation into this country of people of British stock?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I heard it and read it
with a great deal of acclaim. As the hon. member for St. John has said, the United States is practically our only field for immigrants at the present time I am sure the hon. member would not wish us to deny entrance to Canada to citizens of the United States, which is now one of our . Allies?

Are any efforts being
made to secure a larger immigration from the United States?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We, have been carrying on a most active propaganda in the United States. We have had very little immigration from overseas since the war began.

According to the minister, the chairman of the National Service Commission took an active part in securing these farm labourers from the United States. Many of these men were no doubt of enemy origin. The chairman of the National Service Commission is also a prominent member of this House, and only a few days ago he expressed the view that these people should be disfranchised. Does the minister think it is fair that the chairman of the National Service Commission should go over to the United States and induce American citizens of enemy origin to come to Canada and then advocate in this House that even if they become British subjects the franchise should be taken from them. That seems to me to be working at cross purposes altogether, and I do not think it will work out well. Was the hon. member for Calgary speaking on behalf of the Government when he advocated that these people should be disfranchised?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I suppose the hon. member does not speak with any idea that I am here to answer authoritatively for the hon. member for Calgary. That hon. gentleman fearlessly expresses his opinion irrespective of whether the statements he makes are authorized by the Government or not. I suppose the hon. member (Mr. Turriff) is

not trying to fasten culpability on the Immigration Branch for having done what it could to help out the western farmer and bring in a supply of greatly-needed fanm labour. Nor do I know on what information he bases the statement that a number of these men were of enemy-country origin. I am not aware that there were a number of that origin. I understand that a large number were Scandinavians, while many were American-born. Of course, I cannot be responsible for the hon. member for Calgary. I assure the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Turriff) that that hon. gentleman had nothing to do personally with bringing in these immigrants, other than to visit the western provinces, interview the members of the provincial government, and facilitate the holding of a conference of business men and others in the city of Winnipeg to discuss this whole question. Whatever action was taken as a result of that conference was taken in accordance with the wishes of the governments of the three prairie provinces. I sent a couple of inspectors of the Immigration Branch to enter into conference with them. They decided upon a plan of campaign with a view to bringing in a supply of farm labour to meet the great demand. Alarm was felt at one time that we were not going to get a sufficient acreage seeded, in view of the necessity for increased production, by reason of the want of farm help. As the United States was the only place to which we could look for an additional supply, we assisted in the campaign, which was successful. The farmers were supplied, the wishes of the provincial governments were met, and, so far as I know, there has been no objection to what was done.

I am in sympathy with the policy of the hon. minister as carried out; I think it was quite proper to help in bringing in a supply of farm help. But we cannot get nine thousand labouring men from the United States without getting quite a large number who are of enemy-country origin, though now of American allegiance. But I think it unfair to induce these men to come into Canada, holding out to them the hope that they may become Canadian settlers and British subjects, and then hold over them the threat that if they become British subjects in the West they are liable to have the franchise taken from them simply because they originally came from enemy countries.

We find here a member of the House of whom ministers speak in 
extravagantly complimentary terms ' announcing a policy that affects hundreds of my constituents as well as hundreds of the constituents of other members of the House. That hon. member says these men should have taken away from them that consideration which the Dominion of Canada, or the British Empire, gave them in exchange for their oath of allegiance, and that it should be taken away wantonly and without reason. Many of my constituents have a right to ask of me as their representative, and we are their representatives, whether the Government is endorsing the view of the hon. member for Calgary. It is all very well to sidestep the matter and say that the hon. member for Calgary is a very independent man. I am not so sure whether he is or not, but that is absolutely beside the question. He is a Government official, a supporter of the Government, and I understand that he is very closely in the confidence of the Government. The Government has asked that we consider the matter of immigration, which comes very close to this question, and I ask whether the Government endorses the view of the hon. member for Calgary, and whether the member for Calgary spoke with the authority of the Government. The minister refuses to answer. The question is a proper one, and it will not do for the minister to sidestep it in that way. We have a right to know whether the hon. member for Calgary spoke with the approval of the Government and the constituents whom we represent have a right to know that. Let them be called diabolical Austrians, Germans or Turks, we are in a British country now, and we have a right to ask if the member for Calgary had the authorization of the Government in making that statement, and the question should not be sidestepped. If it is going to be sidestepped, we should not go on and vote money for immigration, but we should withhold our sanction for this expenditure until we have some statement from the Government with respect to it. The minister wrote that letter saying that conscription was ,not in force in Canada. He might as well have told them that they were living in America, for they all knew that conscription was not in force. It was absolutely true, but it was a mere platitude. He told them further that the Government was not going to conscribe Americans. What was the object in making such a statement as that? The Government has no power to conscribe Americans. If it con-scribes Americans it means a declaration

of war against the United States. Yet the minister spends his time writing letters declaring that he is not going to put conscription in force against American citizens who may be found within our borders. What an absurd thing! The minister must have meant something in writing such a letter. You might as well say that you are not going to take them for a flight to Mars or Jupiter as to say that you are not going to conscribe American citizens. You could not do so anyway. You might as well declare war against the United States at once. The minister should deal with us frankly when he asks us to pass this vote, and he should answer that simple and fair question whether the member for Calgary spoke with the authorization of the Government or did not. The minister should certainly know what the fact is with regard to that particular matter.	.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Knowles) speaks as if the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett), when he gave this opinion to the House, was laying down the policy of the Government. The member for Calgary was giving the House the benefit of his views as to what the Government should do, but he was giving expression to his own personal views. I am not in a position to say if he spoke with the authority of the Government. On the contrary, I feel convinced he did not. I do not know if the hon. gentleman wants any more direct reply than that. The hon. member states that I have sent a letter all over the country saying that we would not conscript Americans, when they knew that we would not do so. If the hon. gentleman could have induced the American press to take that view, it would not have been necessary to have sent that letter. But in view of the fact that a portion of the American press carried on a grossly misleading campaign on this very point, stating that we wanted to get their men into this country to press them into military service, it was necessary to combat that propaganda, and for that purpose I sent this letter. My action did not provoke any criticism last year. I read the letter in the House last year, and it apparently received the endorsation of every member present. I shall read the letter again.
8th January, 1916.
Through either lack of knowledge or from some ulterior motive numerous papers in the United States have recently advised American citizens that by going to Canada they incurred the risk of being drafted as soldiers in the present world-wide war. Were these articles
confined only to that portion of the pro-German press, which without regard to the truth, have been publishing fictitious news items intended to injure .the trade or stir up friction between the States and Canada, the reports might safely be let go uncontradicted, but when responsible journals are misled into publishing erroneous information regarding conscription it seems advisable to make an official pronouncement upon the matter.
I therefore beg to advise you that all troops from Canada for the war have gone voluntarily; that while the Government has the power to enforce conscription, such action has not been considered either advisable or necessary, - and that even were conscription introduced it would apply to Canadian citizens only.
For your information when dealing with this subject, I may say that many Canadians resident in the United States and many American citizens have crossed into Cajiada since the outbreak of war, have offered their services, been accepted, did valuable work and in ^ some cases gave up their life in the cause of liberty and justice.	.
Any publicity you may care to give to this letter will be appreciated by,
Tours faithfully,
W. J. Roche, Minister of the Interior.
That letter was included in the Canadian Atlas and in our immigration pamphlets that we distributed, and it was for the purpose of counteracting the propaganda that was carried on by a certain portion of the American press. If that letter was foolish and absurd, as the hon. member for Moose-jaw says, I wish to say that I sent it for the reason which I have given. If I had not taken steps to check this misrepresentation that was indulged in among the press, and which brought the Department of the Interior many individual inquiries and. letters, I would have been open to the condemnation that I had not taken the best means available for counteracting it. I do not see why I should be censured for writing that letter for the purpose of counteracting that misrepresentation that American citizens , who came into Canada would be subject to conscription.

It seems to me that the letter is objectionable in that the minister, while he states what everybody knows, that American citizens would not in any circumstances be liable to conscription, yet goes farther and says that it has not been considered at all necessary or advisable by the Government of Canada. What was the object of making that statement? It was to induce American citizens to come in and become permanent settlers in Canada. It was to induce them to become citizens of our country and to take up or buy homesteads, and, in that connection, to allay their fears that the minister clearly held out to them the belief that conscription

would not need to be introduced into Canada, that the Government did not consider it necessary or advisable.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Do not forget the date of the letter.

It was to allay that fear. The minister puts a double proposition forward. First, he says that American citizens would not be liable to conscription under any circumstances, and then he proceeds further to tell them what is the policy of the Government in regard to conscription. If the Government had any notion that conscription would ibe a justifiable and proper policy to pursue in this country he ought not to have made that statement, made, as it was, for the purpose of inducing people to come in from the United States, become permanent citizens of Canada and become also British subjects, because they would have to become British subjects before they could obtain homestead lands and obtain a patent therefor from the Crown. The minister will agree with me that in making that propaganda he intended to go to the extreme limit to allay all possible fears that American settlers might be subject to conscription. If the minister had in his mind, or if the Government had in their minds, at that time, that if this war continued they would introduce conscription into Canada, then the minister ought not to have allayed that fear by writing that letter, because settlers would naturally draw the conclusion from the minister's statement that the policy of the Canadian Government was against, the introduction of conscrip- [DOT] tion. I am very glad to learn that the minister has succeeded in getting a large number of immigrants 'from the United States into Canada last year.
Of course, the number is very small indeed as compared with the number of those who came in during the years preceding 1911. During the period when the late Government was encouraging immigration, settlers came in, not by the thousands but by the hundreds of thousands, from the United States. I should like to see that day^retum. That is what we want in our western country. But in our efforts to get settlers we ought to be very careful not to make any mistakes or misstatements as to existing facts, or as to the policy of the. Government of the day. Nothing would do so much harm to immigration nothing would do so much harm to Canada so far as immigration is concerned, as a, general impression that the Government of this country had not absolutely kept faith with those who

were induced to come into the country. I think that on reflection the minister will feel that in view of the announcements that have been made within the past few days in this House, his statement in regard to conscription was an unfortunate one if, by reason of it, settlers were induced to come into Canada.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
My lion. friend, I am
afraid is drawing a long bow. He overlooks the diate of this letter, January 8,1916.
The war was on then.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
And we were in hopes
that before to-day the war would be over.

On what did the minister base that expectation?
.Mr. ROCHE: If I asked the hon. gentleman now, how soon, in his opinion, the war would be over, what would he say?

I may tell my hon.
friend, and the Minister of Marine will vouch for the statement I make, that my opinion, given very shortly after the war began, was that it would last for a number of years. I never could understand on what ministers acted when they told the people of this country that it would probably be over in three months, nine months or a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Government never told people that.
Mr. PUGSLEY- One o.f the ministers, the other day, said that most people expected that in three months it would be ever.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is a very different
statement.

I have no conception
on what anybody would base that idea. Here was a country, Germany, which, as the evidence has shown, had been preparing for forty years for this war, and how anybody could suppose that Germany could be crushed in one or two years or three years, be worn down or crushed out, tht Prussianism, monarchism in Germany could be is beyond my comprehension. Here, in 1916, when the minister is starting a propaganda in the United States to get settlers to come into this country, not merely getting people for temporary purposes, for the purpose of doing work on the farms, but in order that they might become settlers in Canada; and knowing that they could not acquire patents to homesteads without becoming naturalized citizens, the minister de-

olares to those people in Chicago that the policy of this Government is not to have conscription in Canada. I say that unless the Government had determined upon that course of no conscription they should not have acted in a way which would be calculated to induce these settlers to believe there was a breach of faith in case conscription should be introduced. I repeat that, in my judgment, unless the Government had a settled policy on the subject,, the minister's statement, made while the war was on, that there was no intention of introducing conscription, was neither necessary nor advisable. It was an unfortunate statement to make and one that might mislead the people and induce many to settle in this country under a misapprehension.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Has the hon. gentleman
heard of any grievance on the part of those who came into Canada on that representation?

Do I know? It is too
early to learn that, because conscription has not been enforced as yet. But I should rather suppose that any man who had been induced to come into Canada and had become naturalized in consequence of the statement which the Minister made in Chicago, with the authority of this Government, would have a very just ground of complaint.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It takes three years from the time the man comes into the country and applies for this homestead before he can become a naturalized subject. He cannot become naturalized in the country until he has been in the country three years.

He takes his first step
by applying for a homestead.

I would ask the minister whether in the spring of last year he became aware that conscription would almost surely be necessary in this country. The hon. member for Victoria and Halibur-ton (Sir Sam Hughes) has stated that, in the spring of 1916, the Prime Minister gave him instructions that recruiting was not to be keenly followed up, and we all know that has been the system for a year, go easy and recruit as few as possible; and, as a result, no recruits in any number were secured during the past year. I suppose the minister would know that conscription was going to be necessary as soon as the decision was reached by the Government that recruiting should be let up on. He would then know that in all human probability conscription would become necessary in order to secure the 500,000 men that had been promised. I ask the minister whether, in thn spring of last year, he was also aware of the fact that the Prime Minister had reached a decision which he had communicated to the then Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes), namely, that he desired that they should let up on recruiting.
M. ROCHE:	I am not aware that the
Prime Minister gave voice to any such instruction. In fact, on the contrary, I heard him in his place deny that he ever made such a statement.

Has the minister not
read- the speech of the late Minister of Militia and Defence in which he so stated.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I am telling what the
Prime Minister stated.
Has he read the speech of the ex-minister?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Ye.?, I have read what
the hon. the ex-Minister of Militia stated. On the other hand, we have the reply to that by the Prime Minister. I am going by the Prime Minister's statement.
Then I ask if he contradicts his then colleague, the ex-Minister of Militia?
Oh what nonsense.
