That answer "nonsense" is worthy the minister, but it is not an answer to my question. This is a serious question, whether or not a decision was come to a year ago to ease up on conscription. The Prime Minister says it was not; the ex-Minister of Militia and Defence says it was. I am addressing the colleague of both these gentlemen; he knows them both, and I ask him if he had any information communicated to him such as the ex-Minister of Militia states was conveyed to him in May, 1916. Did the minister have any intimation that there was going to be an easing up of recruiting?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I am quite well aware that no statement was ever issued on the part of the Prime Minister or any member of the Government to the effect that there should be an easing up on the recruiting.

The hon. minister does not mean that there was no statement made by any member, because the Minister of Militia and Defence was a very important

member of the Government, and he so stated.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Did he state that while a member of the Government?
He has stated now that that intimation was made to him.

Does the Minister of
the Interior suggest that he would be more truthful when a member of the Government that he is now?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
doing the suggesting.

I want to say that you have two statements, one by the Prime Minister and one by the ex-Minister of Militia, and only one of them is the truth, because they are directly opposed to each other. But all the corroborative evidence would lead one to judge that the ex-Minister of Militia was telling the truth. I will tell you why. Upon the return to Toronto of a delegation which had come here to interview the Prime Minister, some of its leading members made statements exactly along the line of the statement made by the ex-Minister of Militia. And there is this further corroborative evidence: at the time the ex-Minister of Militia received, as he says, instructions from the Prime Minister to let up in recruiting, recruiting dropped from 25,000 to 5,000 men a month. It looks, therefore, as if the exMinister of Militia was telling the truth. To my mind, explanations should be made not by the ex-Minister of Militia, but by some member of the Government, because there is no doubt that recruiting fell as I have stated. Why should recruiting fall so suddenly if word had not been passed around,-as the ex-Minister of Militia says, on the direct instructions of the Prime Minister,-that there should be a let up in recruiting?

I hope that the minister is not disposed to let a serious statement like this pass without notice. The truthfulness of the ex-Minister of Militia has been emphasized in another way. The exMinister of Militia, in a letter which he ' wrote to the Prime Minister in May, 1915, stated that for three whole months his operations had been blocked by a committee of the Cabinet; that he had not been permitted to proceed with the purchase of trucks because this committee were deliberating as to how the contracts could best be let in order to distribute as much commission as possible among its friends. That [M. Knowles.1
is, I think, as serious a charge as could possibly be made by one member of the Government against his colleagues;- yet neither the Prime Minister nor any other member of the Government has ventured to question this statement of the ex-Minister of Militia. Whatever may be said of the ex-Minister of Militia, I do not believe he can be charged with untruthfulness, and it would require a good deal of evidence and the exercise of exceptionally good memory on the part of members of the Government before they could induce the people to believe that the ex-Minister of Militia deliberately misstated the facts in regard to this very important matter.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock, Mr. Rainville in the Chair.

I asked the minister
some little time ago in regard to advertising done in the United States to induce men to come to Canada for farm work, and he replied that the announcement was that those who worked for farmers this summer would be allowed -six months' residence on their homesteads.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: They would be allowed the time they spent on the farms to count as residence.
Is the minister sure that that offer applied only' to one season's work and did it apply to two seasons' work?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: To 1917 alone.
The minister is absolutely positive on that point?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That is what I am informed. That certainly was the intention.

I was given to understand that in a Seattle newspaper the immigration agent, Mr. Grieve advertised that two seasons' residence could be put in by working with farmers, so that a man takings up a homestead and working for two summers with farmers would have to put in only six months' residence on his homestead [DOT] in order to obtain his patent.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That is not the intention.
That is not correct?
No.

By what authority was
that privilege given?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I am inclined to think it
was done by Order in Council. I am not just sure as to that at the moment.

I would like the minister to inform the House definitely at a later date, because I am under the impression that an Order in Council would not be sufficient; that the Act of Parliament is absolutely explicit as to residence duties to be performed by homesteaders; and my impression is that when the Government undertook to vary the terms of residence, as they admittedly did, they did so absolutely without authority. In my view such variation in regard to homestead duties was absolutely contrary to the public interest, to the well-being of the western country, and to good policy in securing its settlement. If there is one curse greater than another that the actual settler of the West has to put up with, it is that of the non-resident homesteader. That policy of the Government which undertakes to permit non-resident homesteading is not promotive of settlement, but is a most serious detriment to settlement and is a very positive injury to those who are actually in occupation of their homesteads and fulfilling their duties in accordance, not only with the letter, but with the spirit of the law, establishing homes in the country, building up the country, and handicapped in doing so by the holding of vacant land by transient homesteaders, not under the law, but under the authority of a minister.
Dealing with the question of the propriety of citizens of Canada, British subjects who are of alien enemy origin, being deprived of their franchise, I would point out that the Minister of the Interior and his colleagues in the Government, did, as a matter of fact, within the past few months vary the terms of the Land Act, arrogating to themselves an authority that did not belong to them for the purpose of holding out special and unwarranted inducements to people of alien enemy origin if such desired to take advantage of those inducements, and that they, or their supporters at any rate, are not in a position to question the right of such people to the franchise which they have acquired in our country under the laws administered by the minister. The minister has disclaimed all responsibility for the utterances of the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett). Technically I think it may be admitted that he is entitled so to repudiate those utterances, but
as a matter of fact, the hon. member for Calgary occupies the same relation to this Government as does the hon. member for Shellburne and Queens (Mr. McCurdy) or the hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Hugh Clark), except that he does not draw a salary and does not hold a title, but his duties are of the same character or are indeed more of an administrative character; and although when he does make a pronouncement on the floor of the House,. the Government are within their rights when they repudiate it, they are not acting in good faith with the country in doing so. They must in fairness assume a measure of responsibility for that member of Parliament to whom they have delegated duties which at one time were supposed to be important and responsible, who is acting as special commissioner of the Government in regard to those special duties which had special connection with this very matter of the bringing people across the line and necessarily with their rights after they came. This very member of Parliament, occupying this position in connection with the Government, having those important duties and responsibilities, who belches forth on the floor of this House against the exercise of their rights by people who have acquired those rights in all honesty and fairness at the hand of this Government- this very gentleman is himself the active agent, in conjunction with this Government and for the Government, in bringing such people across the line and in offering them, contrary to law, inducements to come here.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
My impression is that this procedure was taken by means of an Order in Council. Such procedure would be under the War Measures Act, and therefore within our jurisdiction. The hon. member says that the minister has repudiated statements made by the hon. member for Calgary. I have not repudiated statements made by the hon. member for Calgary; I was asked by the hon. member for Moose-jaw (Mr. Knowles) if the hon. member for Calgary was authorized by the Government to make the statements he did in his speech when discussing another subject, namely, the Franchise Act. I. stated that so far as I was aware the hon. member for Calgary was not authorized by the Government; that is as far as I have gone; that it is as far, I think, as I am called upon to goi. I am not responsible for the personal views held on this or any other subject by the hon. member for Cal-
174a

gary or any other h-on. member. The hon. member for Calgary has done good service for the Government as chairman of the National Service Commission and in other capacities. He 'has endeavoured to bring the man power of this country to bear on the war to the very best purpose, and as Chairman of the National Service Commission he took up with the various provincial governments the question of the best means of supplying the demand for farm labour. Apart from that, the hon. member for Calgary had nothing whatever to do Iwith bringing these men in from the United States. No special inducements were held out to men of enemy nationality, as the hon. gentleman would lead the House to believe. On the contrary, we issued pos-( itive instructions that men of enemy nationality were not to be admitted.
I said of enemy origin.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The men who came in were citizens either of the United States or of an Allied country, and not citizens of an1 affien enemy country. There are in the United States citizens whose antecedents came from Germany or Austria, but we have these people in Canada as well, and many of them have become naturalized and taken up homesteads here. What would the hon. gentleman have had us do? Would he have had us keep the farm labourers out, although they were citizens of the United States, simply because their antecedents came from Germany or Austria? I do not think the hon. gentleman would have taken that stand; it would have been unreasonable for him to do so.
The hon. gentleman also spoke about the land laws and said we were not warranted in taking the action we did. I can tell him that we have been complimented on holding out this inducement to farm labourers no matter whether they came from the United States or'from any part of Canada. There was such a great demand for farm help in the West, consequent on the heavy enlistments from those provinces, that some steps had to be taken to get farm labourers, and we have been complimented by the hon. gentleman's own political friends in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta for offering to count the time these men spent with a farmer as residence on their own homesteads should they care to fake one up. It is all right for the hon. gentleman to say that we were not warranted in offerfMr. Roche.]
ing this inducement after the demand has been supplied, but if we had not supplied the farm labour the hon. member would have been the first to condemn it, especially at a time when everybody is preaching and diesiring to practise increased production. I do not think the hon. member can hold this Government responsible for any individual opinions the hon. member for Calgary may have expressed on the franchise question. As I have said before, if the hon. gentleman condemns us for holding out this inducement to farm labourers, he is certainly not in agreement with his own political friends in western Canada, for they most assuredly have endorsed the action of the Government in this respect.

I can only say in regard to that what the minister himself says in regard to his colleague: I am not responsible for the opinions of my friends. I take responsibility for stating in my place in this House my opinion of the action of the Government. That action is not only unwarranted and ill-advised, but illegal as well. And that action was taken in pursuance of a policy the logical conclusion of which is condemned by the very men who were parties to it. I did not suggest any, condemnation of the Government because they permitted labourers of alien enemy origin to be brought into Canada. But I condemned the colleague of the Minister of the Interior who refused to recognize the same right of citizenship conferred by this Dominion under the authority of the British Government that the minister says here to-night, and says very properly, he ought to recognize when conferred by the United States of America. As to the assertion that the Government is not responsible for the utterances of their supporter, I reply that when their supporter occupies a responsible position in which he acts on their behalf it is not for the Government to dissociate itself from the utterances of that hon. gentleman in this House in regard to a matter of public policy. Technically, they may be able to do so, but as a matter of fact and as a matter of right they cannot do so. The Minister of the Interior must either shoulder responsibility for the utterances of the hon. member for Calgary, or he must, on behalf of the Government which employs that hon. member, repudiate that hon.'member's sentiments, and this he has not yet done.	*
Now, I wish to ask the minister if the department keeps a record of the movement of people from Canada to the United States.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No. No statistics are kept by the Canadian authorities of those going from Canada to the United States.
Has it ever been the custom of the department to keep such statistics?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.

I remember very distinctly that when my hon. friend. (Mr. Roche) was in opposition his friends, if not himself, were very insistent that such statistics should he kept, and they were very strongly of the opinion that without such statistics the record of immigrants coming into the country was not complete or convincing. At that time the flow of immigration into Canada was very great, the settlement of the country was progressing rapidly and development was going on at a rate never heard of before and certainly never heard of since. At that time possibly it was not important that we should keep account of the people who went out. But, at a time like this, when immigration has languished, when our population is at a standstill, so far as we are aware, it would certainly be of the greatest interest to the Canadian public to know how many people are leaving Canada. I would suggest that, if the minister has not kept such records in the past, he should take means to keep them for the future. Further, while I would not wish to contradict the minister in a matter of his own department, I am still strongly under the impression that at some time such a record as I speak of was kept. Would the minister inquire about that?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I am informed that there has never been any record kept by the Canadian immigration authorities of those leaving Canada for the United States. Nor has any record been kept by the United States of the movement of their population into Canada. Sometimes they ask us for our figures, and sometimes we ask them for theirs. But both Governments act on the same plan-neither keeps a record of the exodus from its country.

I should be sorry to get into an argument with the minister on that point, but I think he will find on inquiry that the United States either did keep or professed to keep a record of the movement of their people into Canada. Such figures have been given in the American report.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: They took our figures.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: No, because it was said that their figures and ours did not agree, and this was brought to the attention of the House by friends of the hon. minister, then in opposition. However, we shall not get very far by arguing that question of fact. But I would point out that during the past year there has been an important movement of people from both eastern and western Canada to the United States. This movement must have been within the cognizance of the officers of the Minister of the Interior. My hon. friend and his officers were absolutely derelict in their duty if they did not take account of that movement. It was stated as a matter of fact that, owing to the announcement made by the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) and the Director of National Service, so-called, there was a very active movement of men eligible for military service from Canada to the United States during the months of October, November, December, and part of January. And, now that I think of it, that movement did come to the attention of the hon. minister and his colleagues. For on the day that Parliament met, or one or two days before or after, a despatch was sent throughout Canada op behalf of the Government, announcing that this movement having taken place because of the fear of military conscription under the so-called national service proposals, this was to assure the people that National Service did not mean conscription for military purposes, and they need not run to the United States in order to get away from it. This movement having been sufficiently important to demand the attention of the Government in the very prominent manner to which I have referred, I say again that the Department of the Interior and its Immigration Branch certainly was asleep at the switch if it did not take cognizance of the volume of that movement. And I say further that, that movement having been caused by the injudicious expressions and declarations of policy on the part of the Prime Minister and his Director of National Service and their newspaper mouthpieces throughout the country, they must take the responsibility for its existence as they took responsibility for attempting to stop it. I wish to point out-and I am sorry the Director of National Service is not here -that though a number of men were brought into Canada ostensibly for farm labour in the West, with a special inducement of non-resident homesteads and special assurance of freedom from conserip-

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: tion, yet the number was not nearly as great as the number of men of like age and capabilities who left the country in the months that I speak of because of the declarations and assertions of the same Director of National Service.

Is the hon. member
speaking of the West now?

I am speaking in large
measure of the province of Ontario. I have in mind the fact that the newspapers of Detroit published an express welcome to 17,000 young Canadians who had recently taken up residence in their fair city.
It was probably better for us that they .should stay in the States, if they went away for that reason.

I quite agree with my hon. friend, and that is precisely why I am pointing out to the minister that it was not sound public policy to offer non-resident homesteading in the western provinces to the same men, or men of a like kind, to bring them back to reside amongst us. That is the policy and practice that I am speaking of, and I hope the hon. gentleman (Mr. Arthurs) will join with me in condemning it.

I had not intended taking part in this debate. But, in listening to the addresses I have gained the impression that hon. gentlemen opposite are barking up two trees at the same time. They are trying, apparently, to play for the German-Austrian vote in the West, and at the same time to condemn the Government for bringing citizens from the United States to help in the harvest. The whole trend of their remarks has been to condemn the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett), for saying that these men who had been only recently, if at all, British citizens, should not be allowed to vote I agree absolutely with the hon. member. I am not speaking for the Government, but for myself, and I have no hesitation in saying what I do though in my own riding there are a good many Germans. But I am not playing one game in one place and a different game in another place. The Minister of the Interior is perfectly justified by the results of the action he took. In the West they were greatly in need of additional farm help, and the minister was justified in bringing in citizens of the United States He could not possibly stop them under international law; the fact that they were citizens of a neutral country precluded us 
from debarring them from Canada. The point of this whole argument, so far as I can see, is only that some hon. members are anxious to secure the support of these men whom they are condemning the Government for bringing in.
My hon. friend (Mr. Arthurs) has a logic of his own.
So have you.

I agree with that, but it certainly is not the same as the hon. gentleman uses. He says we are barking up two trees at the same time What is the Government doing? According to the announcement of their friends, they are going to disfranchise these people who are ot Austrian and German origin.

The Government did
not announce that.

Through their director of National Service. And the Government have no right to repudiate those whom they trust with important duties of that kind. At the same time, they are claiming credit for disposing of their lands in the Northwest in order to bring back the very men which the loose talk of the Director of National Service was driving across the line. The Government and its friends should take either one side or the other. They should speak of what they intend to do, or they should hold their tongues. They should not talk of conscription unless they intend to enforce it; and if they intend to enforce it, they should enforce it not talk about it. And when they talk about disfranchising citizens of this country because of their origin, they should not at the same time offer special inducements to people of the same origin but of United States nationality to come in and occupy our lands on terms unfair to our own settlers.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if any great- proportion of those men who came over to work on the farms of the West were such citizens as he has described here?

I do not know who ot
what they were but there is no reason to suppose that they were not. The Minister of the Interior has assured my hon. friend that if they were .of that character they wo-uld not have been stopped from coming.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: They were American citizens.
They were American citizens. Why should not British citizenship be just as good and get the same rights as United States citizenship at the hands of this Government?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Kings, Prince Edward Island (Mr. Hughes) asked if we would extend the same privileges to Prince Edward Islanders who might go out West and I said: Yes, certainly. If they came from the United States they would have been United States citizens of British nationality but if they came from any of the other provinces of the Dominion they would have 'been given the same privilege.

A United States citizen of alien enemy origin was given by the Director of National Service, under the authority of the Minister of Interior, the special privilege of non-resident homesteading in the Northwest while the same Director of National Service was declaring that a man of British citizenship but of the same alien enemy origin should be disfranchised.
Is the same privilege of non-resident homesteading given to men resident in Canada who might go out and work on the farms in the West?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Certainly.

Are any inducements
given to residents of the other provinces to go West?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The same.
Was any advertising resorted to in order to make the facts known?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It was advertised in the
press of the country. The privileges were extended to people from any province in the Dominion.
Does the minister know if any considerable number went from the Canadian provinces?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We did not encourage them to go from the other provinces for the reason that we were informed that in all the other provinces they were just as badly off as they were in the West.
How many homestead entries were taken up during the past year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: During the fiscal year ended March 31, 1917, the total number of homestead entries was 11,199.

It appears that 70,000 settlers came in, but only 11,000 homesteads
were taken uip. Has the minister any information as to whether the others only came temporarily, or whether they bought land, or went into the cities? ,

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The 60,000 who came in from the United States included men, women and children, and, of course, children are not supposed to take up homesteads.
Still, immigrants as a rule do not bring in many children.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes, they come in with quite large families.
In what provinces were these 11,000 homesteads taken up?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The three prairie provinces' and particularly in the northern part of Alberta.
In the Peace River district?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: A great many went into the Peace River district.
Are there many available homesteads having good soil in that part of Alberta south of the Saskatchewan river?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: South of that latitude there are no large blocks of land still available and not disposed of. There is land here and there, but no large amounts, such as a township. There is comparatively little in Alberta south of Edmonton.
I do not mean townships, but is there any considerable extent of good land still open for homesteading south of the Saskatchewan river?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Comparatively little.

The reason I ask the minister is that he has upon the Order Paper a proposal, of which a good deal of notice has 'been taken, and which proposal was put forward to a committee in England by the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) to assist returned soldiers to take up homesteads and give them a loan of money. What I was desirous of knowing was whether, in order to avail themselves of this offer, settlers would have to go north of the Saskatchewan. From what the minister says, I judge that will be substantially correct.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: To get blocks of land of any extent they will have to go to the northern part of the province.
Did I understand the minister to give the number of homestead entries during the past year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
How many?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior

speechtext: I take it that the expenditure on immigration is primarily for the purpose of securing settlement on homesteads. Am I right?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We are particularly desirous of getting those who wish to locate upon the land and we are making a special effort to secure farmers, farm labourers and domestic servants.

The expenditure is largely for the purpose of securing homestead settlement. I think we all agree that that is right. We find that during the past year the efforts of the immigration department resulted in securing 11,000 homesteaders, and I find, on referring to the figures, that in 1910-11 and 1911-12 we had in the neighbourhood of 44,000 homesteads taken, or four times as many as we had in this past year. I suppose that that would argue that there was four times as much work done by the immigration department; at any rate, the results of the work done were four times as great as they were last year. I wish to point out, in the same line of reasoning, if my hon. friend over here (Mr. Arthurs) will permit me, that 1 used the other night in regard to the estimates of the lands branch, that the expenditure by the Department of the Interior in regard to immigration in this time of war, when we are voting half a million dollars for war expenditure, is extravagant beyond all reason, because we are spending this year, according to this estimate, considerably more money than we did in the year 191011, or the year 1911-12, when we were securing four times as many homestead settlers. I desire to emphasize that this Government in all its departments, and certainly in its Interior Department, does not know that there is a war on or that this country, in view of the extraordinary expenses of the war, demands that the expenses for the ordinary services of the country be cut down in accordance with the war conditions which reduce the possibility of results from those services. We have actually increased our expenditures for these services, notwithstanding the tremendous demands made upon ue by the war. Here is this instance, the Immigration Department demands 11,215,000 for the year 1917-18, and in the year 1910-11 the demand was for $1,040,000, and for 1911-12, for $1,066,000. The only difference in the service is that in those 
years we paid $15,000 to the Winnipeg and St. Boniface hospitals, and in this year that sum does 'not appear, but there is $29,000 for Chinese immigration. The Minister of the Interior convicts his Government of absolute extravagance and of disregard of war conditions.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I may tell the hon. gentleman that he is away off in his figures. He states that we do not know that there is a war on, viewing it from the standpoint of the expenditure of the Immigration Branch, and that we have not 'been reducing our expenditure.
No, I say your expenditure is out of proportion to the result of your work.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
qualifying the impression that he conveyed to the House, that we have not taken any steps to reduce the expenditure because of the war being on- I beg to say that his figures are not quite accurate as to the actual expenditure in 1910-11. For the year 1911-12, which was the last year the hon. gentleman prepared- the estimates for the Immigration Department, the expenditure was $1,354,736, and the expenditure of this past year has been $1,152,275.

How many people
came in 1910?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The people who came in
1910-11 were 311,084.
And last year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior

speechtext:
I took my figures
from the public accounts; I have them here.
Mr. RO(5hE:	I do not think the hon.
gentleman will find such figures in the public accounts.

I have them here.
I compared* the figures of 1910, which were $1,079,000, and those of 1915-16 which were $1,307,000.	.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The hon. gentleman said four years ago, my attention was drawn to his remarks in Hansard; he said that the Minister of the Interior was spending $300,000 more now for immigration than four years 'ago.
The hon. gentleman must realize that I was referring to the last year of the Liberal administration

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Four years ago. It is
$700,000 less to-day. The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) was quoting the estimates for last year and said we had spent $1,574,000.
I beg pardon, I did not quote the estimates of last year.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Was he referring to the estimates of the present year?
Yes, this year.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The estimates of this year are considerably below last year, nearly $300,000. So I think there cannot be any charge-
Will the hon. gentleman say how the deduction of $300,000 was made up?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
By sweeping reductions all along the line. In some instances by the reduction of the staff. Where offices would become vacant in many instances we did not fill them, and we have had reductions
all along the line. And it is a substantial reduction below last year, $300,000, and below four years ago, $700,000.

I find on reference to the public accounts that the expenditure on immigration in 1910-11 was $1,079,129; and in 1915-16, $1,307,480, an increase of $238,351. I say that increase of expenditure, with the decreased business done, is absolutely indefensible, and I wish to say further that when the minister talks about decreasing his expenditure from one million eight hundred thousand down to one million whatever it is this year, I would respectfully ask him on what ground he increased it from $1,079,000 in 1911 to $1,800,000 in 1914. Under what possible state of circumstances could he justify that enormous increase at that time and in that period?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We had a very large immigration continuing until the outbreak of the war, and then immigration did drop; the overseas immigration since then has been almost a negligible quantity. But we have had other expenditures in connection with immigration which the hon. gentleman did not have to the same extent, because it is only of comparatively recent years that we have instituted this rigid system of boundary inspection. It was done before the hon. gentleman left office, but we have had to increase the boundary inspection and during the war we have had to put on an additional number of boundary inspectors to watch the boundary and assist other departments in their work. Our boundary inspectors have been called upon to do considerably more work since the war broke out, and that work has increased very materially. In England all our immigration agencies have been maintained, and we have carried on a much more active propaganda in the United States. The hon. member, being a journalist himself, realizes how very much more expensive it is to get out literature; paper is higher, labour is higher, our advertising is higher, and getting out literature is in every way much more expensive.
We have spent a great deal more money in the United States than we did prior to the outbreak of war. We have made special efforts to get immigration from the United States since we were shut off from overseas immigration.
Has the minister kept up the work of the repatriation of Canadians?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
What was done last year?

Colonization agents visit
*the New England states and bring back and locate in the various provinces French Canadians or their descendants who had gone across the line. These 9 p.m. agents, who report to the department frpm time to time, claim to have met with a considerable degree of success in their work. They have located some of these persons in Northern Ontario, Northern Saskatchewan, Northern Alberta and some in the province of Manitoba.
.Mr, MARCIL:	Has the minister any
figures as t,o the number of persons brought in last year as a result of this work?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The figures are not separated from the general statistics. They are contained in the reports sent in by the colonization agents.
How many of these agents have you in the United-States.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: These are special colonization agents who visit the New England states and act in conjunction with our established agencies there. We have eight of them.
What are their names and their places of residence?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: J. E. Robillard, Lanoraie, Que., $1,500; G. C. Poulin, St. Johns, Que., $1,200; Odilon Rathe, Henryville, $1,200; J. B. L. Bourassa, Montreal, $1,200; J. B. H. Giroux, Montreal, $600; J. A. Norman-deau, Montreal, $600 ; 0. Corbeil, Montreal, $600; Napoleon Poirier, Bellegarde, Sask., $600.

What kind of work does the hon. minister expect a man to do at $600 a year, in view of the high cost of living?
iMr. ROOHE: Is the hon. gentleman objecting to the salaries being so low? Does he desire that they be increased?
I was wondering what the minister expected a man to do at a remuneration of $600 a year.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I understand that they are satisfied with the .salaries.
Are they expected to give 12 months of their time for $600?
They are allowed certain travelling expenses in addition to their salaries.
Wihat did these additional expenses amount to last year?
They are published in the Auditor General's report.
The minister mentioned the name of M. Poirier of Bellegardie, Sask. What does M. Poirier do, aside from the work to which the minister has referred?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: He is a clergyman.

What is the minister
doing in the way of bringing labouring men for the farms into the province of Ontario?

The province of Ontario
has received a fair proportion of the farm help that has come in; it has its own immigration organization as well. The special agents sent to the United 'States by the province of Ontario this spring have been acting in co-operation with our agents there. I understand that quite a number of farm labourers-I do not know Ihow many-have come to the province of Ontario this spring.

I do not know of any; certainly none have come into our section of the country. I was wondering if the minister was doing anything in this respect, because we have been very short of farm labour in Ontario. The department used to pay certain persons, who were not given a regular salary, so much for every man that they placed on the farms. I3 that work still carried on?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
Who is doing that work in the county of Oxford?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Samuel Nagle, Ingersoll; F. W. Burgess, Woodstock; Thos. Milson, Tavistock; Messrs. Hollier and Walsh, Til-sonburg; John Pollock, Norwich; Sam L. Foe, Richmond, and Richard Hanson, Tavistock.
Who in the world is F. W. Burgess?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I can not tell the hon. gentleman who he is, but his name appears as one of those colonization agents who is paid $2 for every farm labourer he places in the province of Ontario.
I do not know him. A man by the name of Burgess is engaged in the sewing machine business in Woodstock; surely it is not he?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I do not know, I am
sure.
Such a man would not be in touch with the farmers.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Perhaps the farmers would be in touch with him.

They might be in touch with him the wrong way. A man by the name of Burgess was turnkey in the jail, but he is dead. A Mr. Irving was engaged in that work, but he died recently, and I was wondering who took his place. I wish my hon. friend would ask his department to make inquiries as to who F. W. Burgess is. I am not speaking from a political standpoint when I say that the minister should engage for this work men who are in touch with the farmers.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The work .these men were appointed to do has fallen off very materially since overseas immigration ceased. They were largely engaged in placing men who had come across the ocean and located on the farms in Ontario.

Can the minister give me
information with regard to the work done by Mr. Wilmot of the Fredericton agency? The office there costs about $2,000 a year.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: While Mr. Wilmot, I understand, has been doing a good deal of work along this line, he was not on the pay-list of the department during the past year.
Is he not now employed by the Government?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
He is doing the work I
understand. I am informed that he is very much interested in the work and he is quite willing to continue to work without salary.

He is doing work without
salary now?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

There is no Fredericton
agency at the present time?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.

In regard to a matter that
was brought up by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) have you any report of work done by Mr. Hay, the Woodstock agent, during the past year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Mr. Hay was under discussion here prior to six o'clock. He sends in to the department his diaries giving particulars as to his work. We have nothing here as to what he has done during the past year. My private information is that Mr. Hay was doing good work, acting in cooperation with the provincial land settlement board, locating, settlers on the land. An hon. member stated this afternoon that Mr. Hay was in the pay of the provincial government. I was unaware of that fact, and I promised to make some further inquiries with regard to the matter.

I know nothing personally about this matter, and I was rather surprised when I heard the statement made by my hon. friend from Carleton regarding this man's salary, and I think the minister must have been mistaken or else I misunderstood him this afternoon when he said that Mr. Hay did not receive anything but his salary. I see by the Auditor General's report of last year that Mr. Hay received besides his salary four hundred and some odd dollars for travelling expenses.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: What year is that?
The Auditor General's Report for the year ended March 31, 1916.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I was speaking of later
than that.

I am referring to the year
of the Auditor General's Report that is in the hands of hon. members, and from that report I find that last year Mr. Hay received $1,963.30 for his services. In view of what my hon. friend said this afternoon with regard to this gentleman's work-
Mr. Hay got $1,900 more than he was entitled to.

I know nothing personally
about this man, but it seems to me that as this money is being spent in the province of New Brunswick, we should have some person doing some work in the interest of colonization and the money should not be thrown away.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I am given to understand
that Mr. Hay has made a trip to the United States for the purpose of securing immigrants.

He made a special trip
with his wife to California. He attended a fair of some kind.
In war time?
Yes, in war time.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That does not at all contradict what I stated. The hon. gentleman is trying to leave the impression that Mr. Hay took his wife to California on a pleasure trip and oharged up his expenses to the Government.
I do not think there is any doubt about that.

I am serious in regard
to the matter.

I would like to put on Hansard what the minister has been doing. In 1910-11, this country expended $1,079,129.85 on immigration and in that year there came to Canada 311,084 people. In the fiscal year ended March 31, 1916, my hon. friend spent $1,307,480.46 on immigration and with that increased expenditure of some $228,000 my hon. friend succeeded in getting 48,537 people to Canada. From my hon. friend's immigration work, it seems that the moTe money he spends the fewer immigrants he secures. I do not know whether .that is a splendid rule to apply for the purpose of economy in war time or not, but perhaps the minister is acting according to the wordis of the Minister of Finance who always declares that no matter what shortcomings the Government have committed at any time and under any circumstances, everything is done for the purpose of winning the war. My hon. friend was throwing away the . money of the people of Canada to the extent of $228,000 a year and he was getting only 48,000 immigrants, whereas, under the guidance of my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), and with a much smaller expenditure, over 311,000 people were induced to come into Canada. My hon. friend was good enough to refer to my criticism with respect to these expenditures, and my figures, I think, are somewhat illuminating and will lead the House and the country to realize just what kind of reckless administration my hon. friend is carrying on in his department.
Has the minister the figures of the immigration for 1912, 1913, 1914 and 1915?

Yes; the immigration for 1912-13 was 402,432; for 1913-14, 384,878. Then the war came on and in 1914-15 the immigration was 144,789. In 1915-16 the immigration was 48,537,when the overseas immigration practically ceased and in 1916-17 the immigration, largely from the United States, amounted to 75,374.

How many came
from Great Britain in 1916-17?

And the balance
from the United States?

Mostly, there were some
from the Continent.
Has the minister the expenditures from 1912 and 1913?

In 1912-13 the expenditure was $1,399,954, and in 1913-14, $1,859,671. The expenditure has been considerably reduced every year since the outbreak of war. For the coming year the expenditure will be $700,000 less than it was four years ag6.
There was an increase of about half a million dollars between 1912-13 and 1913-14, and a decrease of immigration of over 17,000.

It is impossible to figure immigration as costing so much per capita, because we have our standing expenditures that are running on. Some years, for instance, we have increased expenditure for literature. Our literature perhaps is going out in very large quantities this year, while next year that item will be considerably less, and it is impossible to judge accurately as to the expenditure being so much by reason of so many immigrants coming in. .
I notice the estimate for immigration last year was $630,000. Was that whole amount spent last year?
No, of last year's estimate we expect to save approximately $400,000.

Before six o'clock I stated that I thought there were half a dozen immigration officers in the vicinity of this Mr. Hay, and the information I received from the minister was that there were none in the county of Carleton. I have here the Auditor General's Eeport for the year 191516. Of course, I do not know what may have taken place since the 31st day of March, 1916, but there has not been very much of a change unless it be upwards. I would like to call the minister's attention to this. I stated that I thought there was an agent at Debec junction,: which is only eleven or twelve miles from Woodstock. There you have Mr. E. E. Kennedy, with a salary of $900, and expenses of uniform suit, $20; meals, $55.20; sundry outlay, $7.26, making a total of $982.46.
I come next to a place called Eichmond, N.B., only six miles from Woodstock. There you have an inspector named Daniel Barrington, at $300. At Oentreville, a few miles north of Woodstock, is A. C. Gibson, with a [DOT]salary of $79.44. So there you have three

men all around Woodstock. I think, perhaps, they are doing something, although there may be a little less to do than some years ago. These men, who are really looking after immigration (business, are getting salaries ranging from $79.44 to $900, and yet this other man, who is simply a Conservative organizer, is getting nearly $2,000 a year; that is the objection I have to make. I think I am justified in bringing this matter up and asking the minister to cut this item out, or at least to make a thorough investigation before he proceeds with it. All along the boundary line, at Grand Falls, St. Leonards, Canterbury, McAdam Junction, . St. Stephen, there are immigration officials receiving from $300 to $900 a year. I admit these men are doing something. They are at the proper location, and I am not asking that their services be dispensed with, but here is a man receiving this enormous salary and doing absolutely nothing. I am sure if the minister looks up this man's diaries he will find he has done practically nothing. I was sure when I made my statement this afternoon that there were other officials in that district, and I have now given the minister the names. He will find them in the Auditor General's Report for 1916, pages K-36, 38, 39, 40.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There must be a misunderstanding. We were discussing whether Mr. Hay occupied the position of colonization agent in the county of Carleton. The men whose names the hon. gentleman has mentioned are boundary inspectors. There are quite a number of them in the province of New Brunswick.
If there are any more in the county of Carleton I should like to have their names.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The list for the province of New Brunswick is as follows:	Willard
Tucker, H. G. Maloney, W. H. Smith, C. H. Maxwell, R. W. Whitlock, R. O'Shaugh-nessy, H. W. Cleland, R. E. Kennedy, D. H. Purinton, E. W. Larlee, C. A. Kirkpatrick, F. A. Roy, L. R. Belanger, W. T. Perron, Thomas Levesque, A. C. Gibson, W. H. Hawthorne, J. A. Newman, Alvin Parker, Jos. B. Porter, O. Robinson, W. E. Spike, J. Theriault, T. H. Wetmore, J. J. Walsh.

I am not finding any
great fault with the appointment of these *gentlemen because they are located at points where people might come into the province, and they are rendering some service for their salaries. I would like to know whether Mr. C. A. Kirkpatrick of Grand Falls has been receiving his salary during the past year. I see he received a salary of $900 and the ordinary perquisites for the year ending March, 1916.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Mr. Kirkpatrick's name is on the list of our inspectors, and he has been drawing his salary of $900 during the past year.
Does the minister know whether he has been performing the services of his office or not?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Most assuredly he has, if he has been drawing his salary.

The minister may be surprised, but I can tell him that this man has only been in Grand Falls once or twice in the last two or three years on a visit. I don't want to say anything unpleasant, but I will say this much; this man is an officer in the King's army who has belonged to various units since he enlisted, and he has never left Canada. I wanted to know whether he was still receiving his salary from the Immigration Department.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: He would be treated on exactly the same terms as others who enlisted before November, 1915.
A few days ago I asked for information in regard to enlistments from the Interior and Indian Departments. Could the minister tell me when I may receive the return?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I am informed that it will soon be ready.

I should be glad if the
minister would expedite it as much as possible.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I will.

I understood the minister to say that Mr. Hay was doing work with the Farm Settlement Board in New Brunswick. As I understand it, the Farm Settlement Board is purely a provincial .organization, which is concerned with the placing of settlers on the land. I cannot understand how Mr. Hay, a Dominion official, should have anything to do with provincial funds expended under this board.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I do not suppose the hon. gentleman objects to the Dominion Government paying Mr. Hay for doing colonization work. We are paying other gentlemen for doing similar work in other provinces. If

it is a fact that Mr. Hay is in the employ of the provincial government, I quite agTee that he should not be drawing a salary from the Dominion Government as well.

I was not objecting to the
salary at all. I had not heard of the gentleman until my hon. friend from Carleton spoke of him. My point was that the Farm Settlement Board was entirely a provincial matter, with which the Dominion Government had nothing to do.
Has any one been appointed temporarily in the place of Mr. Kirkpatrick at Grand Falls since he enlisted?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I cannot say offhand, but I can get the information fpr our next sitting.
Who is the immigration agent at Edmonton South?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Mr. Clegg is at Edmonton, Alberta. That is the only one at Edmonton that is given in the list before me.
What duties are performed by Mr. Fielding, of Windsor, Nova Scotia, whose name appears in the Auditor General's Report as immigration agent there?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: He is not now-in the employ of the department.
He is one of the men dropped last year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
Has anybody been appointed in his place?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.
Is T. J. Webb still in the employ of the Government at Anti-gonish?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: He is not now in the employ of the department.
I understand the Windsor office is abolished?	*
Yes.
Who is the immigration agent at Grande Prairie?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have not in the list before me the name of any officer located at that point.	-

There is an immigration hall at Grande Prairie for which the department pays a rental of $65 a month. There

are a considerable number of people going in, and I was curious to know to what extent the hall was being utilized. It seems strange that we should pay rent for a hall and have no one to look after it.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The hall is being utilized and a caretaker is in charge, but I have not his name before me.

A hall for immigrants will not take care of itself, and if the building is to be utilized-and I assure the minister it is desirable that it should be utilized, as a considerable number of immigrants are going in at that point-if there is not some person taking care of the hall the minister should make arrangements to have some person in charge. I believe that for some time the department was paying rental for this hall, and that, as it was not needed for immigration, it was being used for other purposes. But at present there is need for immigration accommodation at that point. I hope that the former condition does not prevail, but that the hall, which is not an unsuitable building for the purpose, is used and is properly taken care of.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The hall is utilized and some person is in charge, who is paid out of contingencies.
I have a question on the Order Paper, but, perhaps, the minister can give me the answer now. What number of people will this hall accommodate, and is sleeping accommodation provided?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It is a small building and not as suitable as we would like. I think there are nine beds in it. I understand the Public Works Department are negotiating for a more suitable place.

I did not inspect the building personally, but from the cursory view I had of it I should not say it was wholly unsuitable, and I should have thought that a larger number of beds than nine could be arranged in it. I suggest to the minister that he should take cognizance of the fact that there is a demand for immigration accommodation at this point, and that while he is arranging for his new building the present building should be utilized in the fullest reasonable measure. Grande Prairie is a railway terminal point in an area that is receiving a great deal of immigration attention and is a proper point for suitable immigration accommodation.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We do not desire to make an appropriation for a new building of this kind. Some negotiations have been carried

on for the renting of the Empire hotel there, which, I understand, would be a very good building for our purposes. If it can be secured at reasonable rates- we think it would be much better to take it for the next two or three years.

Following up my question with regard to Strathcona, I see by the Auditor ' General's Report that Adolphe Adam is named at a salary of $1,314. Can the minister inform me if Mr. Adam is still on the payroll?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I am inclined to think he is not. His name is not on the list before me as that of one of the officials at that point.

Is the minister aware of the reason why Mr. Adam is not on the payroll?
, Mr. ROCHE: I am pretty sure his services were dispensed with.

While I do not wish to interfere with the minister's plan, I desire to say that in my judgment, if suitable arrangements can be made with regard to the Empire hotel at Grande Prairie, as it is a large building and moderately new, I think it would be wise to make arrangements for it as quickly as possible. Now is the time when the people are going in and the time when they need the accommodation. Two or three months from now they will not be going in. The present building, I should think, is not large enough to accommodate the people going in. -So if there is to be a change the quicker the better.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I understand an officer was sent in there several days ago to try and get a building.
I am glad to hear it. I think there was an appropriation for an immigration hall at Spirit River.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I understand there is to be an immigration hall at that point. I think the Public Works Department have an appropriation in for its construction.

There are three points in the Peace River country that are receiving a very considerable immigration at the present time. There is, first, Grande Prairie, which is the terminal point of the railroads and from which radiates a settlement perhaps 60 miles in length by 25 miles in breadth. Then there is Spirit River, which is a smaller settlement and which is at the junction of the Grand Prairie branch railway. I do not know that there is any accommodation provided at the present time.
I am under the impression that there is not, but I believe an appropriation was taken for the construction of a hall. I would be very glad to see a hall erected at Spirit River. The erection of the hall, if it is in progress now, will not be of very much present value. There are people going to that point at the present time and I would suggest that the minister take cognizance of the situation at Spirit River and secure, if possible on reasonable terms, immigration accommodation at that point without delay. I would like to say a word also regarding Peace River. Peace River is the terminus of the railroad on the Peace river and is the railway point for a settlement 60 miles in length and with prospects of growing up and down the river. I do not think there is any immigration accommodation at that point at the present time and I would urge upon the minister the desirability of securing, again if it is possible on reasonable terms, immediate temporary accommodation with the view of establishing permanent accommodation at whatever later date circumstances will permit. Grand Prairie, Spirit River and Peace River are all urgent in the matter of immigration accommodation during the present season.
I understood the minister to say that the Fredericton agency had been abolished. Am I right?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
That is where Mr. Wilmot
is?
Yes.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I stated that Mr. Wilmot
asked to be allowed to continue doing his work but without pay.

I am not speaking of
Mr. Wilmot alone but of the whole agency. I find a couple of names here in the Auditor General's Report-F. E. Fenety, assistant agent, $1,000 a year; a stenographer, Miss Thomas, $600 a year; a janitor, office expenses, etc.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I believe these are on the list yet.

That is what I think.
What office do they rent in Fredericton and to whom do they pay the rent?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I will have to take a note of the question of my hon. friend as I am not personally aware of the circumstances.

While the amount is not very great, the remarkable thing about it is that there was a building erected in Fredericton some years ago as a post office and customs house. It was plenty large enough for a city the size of Fredericton for a good many years to come. But, a few years ago this Government, in its wisdom, erected another building immediately alongside of the old building at a cost of about $150,000. It seems rather remarkable that you have to go and hire an outside office to get public accommodation in the little city of Fredericton. It seems extraordinary that you have to pay $105 for office expenses and janitor when you have such splendid accommodation in Fredericton.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have no personal knowledge of the building or as to who owns it, or what rent we pay for it, but I will take note of what the hon. gentleman has stated and make inquiries. Does the hon. gentleman know who owns the building?

No, I do not. but I have a very shrewd suspicion. I do not want to mention any names without feeling sure of them. I would be very much obliged to the minister if he would look into the matter and let us know who is receiving this small honorarium, because there is no office being occupied, and I doubt very much if there is any janitor being employed.
What position does Mr. Fenety hold there?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Assistant.
Last year he was assistant, but if there is no principal I do not see how there can be an assistant.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
This gentleman has been
there for some time and his services have been retained. Mr. Wilmot was informed that we would have to dispense with his services and we were about to close the office but the proposition was put up by Mr. Wilmot that he would be glad to give what services he could personally without charging any remuneration for himself. It is absolutely impossible to close the office entirely. I do not think he has any personal financial interest in having the office ' retained.

I have no objection to
Mr. Fenety and Miss Thomas receiving their salaries, but it is an absolutely useless waste of public money. They are not doing anything because there is nothing to

do and there never has been anything to do. There was a time when Mr. Fenety was interested to some extent in what they called the Farm Settlement Board, but it ceased to exist as an immigration factor three or four years ago. I do not think I am revealing any political secrets when I tell you that it will absolutely cease to exist in the course of a very short time because there has been a change in the affairs of New Brunswick within the last three months. As an immigration agency there is nothing doing, nothing has been done and nothing will be done, and unless my hon. friend wishes to keep these two people employed-the amount is not very great-he had better cancel the whole thing and get rid of the agency.

In what foreign
country has the minister Canadian agencies other than the United States?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We have no agencies now in any foreign country that I can recollect. We had one in Copenhagen. That has been closed since the war. We had one at Antwerp and that- also has been closed. We had a Paris agency also. The foreign agencies have been closed except those in the United States.
What is the expense of the Paris office?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: In France there has been a very slight expenditure. We have a clerk, Mr. Martin, at $660 and a typist, Mrs. M. Martin, at $720, so that the total salaries there axe $1,380.

I am glad that my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has raised thfis question about the different agencies in foreign countries. It seems to me that the Minister of the Interior should state the policy to be pursued by the department after the war as regards those European agencies. I concede that the best immigrants we can secure for the country are the Americans-, although it is very difficult to draw a distinction between the American born and the foreigner who has settled in the United States. That may give rise to very serious difficulties in view of the problem which was raised a few days ago on the question of the franchise. The Government ought to have a polficy for the period after the war. I put aside -at once the question of encouraging immigration from the Central Powers to Canada. It would be a great mistake to attempt to attract to Canada people from Germany

or from Austria. But, although the losses caused by this war will be enormous and although there will be, on the part of those countries devastated by the war, a desire to keep their nationals wttthin their own boundaries, yet, wife millions remaining and with the horrors that the present war will have left in the minds of the present and the coming generations, it is to be hoped that thousands and hundreds of thousands will, after the war, seek a refuge and a home in America.
Of all the countries that we as Canadians must rely upon for an excellent stock, I shall name first the British Islands. I do not know to what extent immigration will come from the British Isles, but I daresay it will be far easier to secure immigrants from them than from any other countries because it seems that after the Conference which has taken place of late during the visit of the ministers to London the tendency in England will be to encourage Britishers to settle in the various dominions and colonies. That immigration will, of course, be welcomed to Canada. But we have other countries also to which we may look as fields for immigration. I hope, in spite of what has been said, that we may expect a large flow of immigration from little Belgium. We all know that Belgium is too small a country, geographicaly speaking, to contain its relatively large population. We were given some months ago, during a debate in this House, a statement of the number of people per square mile in Belgium. It is something appalling to think of the number of people who have to dwell on the few thousands of acres which comprise the area of little Belgium. It seems to me that the Belgians, who are such hard workers and such excellent operators, and especially such good farmers and gardeners, should be encouraged to come to Canada. I am not sure that the Minister of the Interior should not take advantage of the fact that at the present moment there are thousands, and I may say hundreds of thousands, of Belgians in England, and try to get some of those good immigrants for Canada.
It is very difficult to expect a large flow of immigration from France. Before the war even, it was difficult to attract settlers from France, and after the war it will be still more difficult, because so many thousands of young men have been mowed down * since 1914. But still, from what I learn from my correspondents in France, it is remarkable how many Frenchmen would be pleased to come to Canada if they could receive the
necessary encouragement from this Government. Some years ago a policy was inaugurated by the Government which gave excellent results. I remember the day when immigration to Canada from France was practically nil. But with a system of advertisement and with good immigration officers in Paris and in the various centres of France, a relatively large number of French immigrants came to Canada.
There are also immigrants of the best quality to be had from the, northern section of Italy. I do not say that the southern section of Italy would be a proper field for Canadian immigration effort, but I do say that the northern part of Italy is an excellent field for securing immigrants. There is a large body of good farmers in that section of Europe. Some years ago a number of them came to Montreal and settled on the island, and I may say that to-day the most prosperous gardeners, and indeed the most wealthy gardeners, in that district are Italians. They come from around Milan and Turin, and have been quite a success in their farming venture on the island of Montreal. I hope that my hon. friend will add a little more to his expenditure for immigration officers in Paris. A well-managed, well,equipped agency at Paris, which is an important European centre, which send to Canada quite a large number of immigrants. I hope that the Government will soon announce its policy concerning immigration after the war.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is probably aware of the fact that the French Government are not in favour of our carrying on an active propaganda for the encouraging of emigration. They do not like to see their settlers emigrate; what we have done in France, therefore, has had to be done very diplomatically. Unfortunately, the gentleman who was our agent there enlisted and was killed. We have not been spending much money on this work in France. We have been doing some advertising, but it has had to be done in such manner as not to attract too much attention, We would not be permitted to carry on an active propaganda such as we do, for instance, in the British Isles. I understand that a proposal has been made by or on behalf of Mr, Roy, who is acting under the Prime Minister's Department, that the immigration staff be merged with that of his office. The immigration authorities, however, find that it is better that matters affecting immigration should be dealt with by a separate branch. In London at one time the immigration business was largely

handled through the High Commissioner's Office, but it was thought that the work would be done more advantageously and with less red tape and restriction if it was dealt with by a separate immigration branch. As to Belgium, it is not in favour of even the refugees coming across the ocean. The authorities there want to keep their own people in their own land in order to build up their devastated country after the war is over. Several offers have 'been made by Belgian priests to come over and act as colonization agents. By reason of communications which we had received from Belgium discouraging any attempts on our part to secure immigration from that country, I did not encourage this proposal. We have felt that we should not do anything opposed to the wishes of the Belgian people, especially with regard to attracting people from their own country during the war. As to an after-the-war policy, we have not yet matuied any particular scheme. We think there is plenty of time, our information being that a large portion of the first year after the war will be occupied in bringing tack our own soldiers, having regard to th" facilities of (transport. An after-the-war pol't-y of immigration, however, has been under consideration, in respect not only of Britain, but of other countries as well. It will be formulated in due time; certain reforms may be adopted, and in connection with after-the-war conditions, the remarks of my hon. friend will be given full consideration.

Because of certain correspondence that I have received, I am aware that my hon. friend has done his best with regard to the French immigration office during the war. I hope that after the war he will see that the immigration office in France shall be properly equipped. Has my hon. friend been interviewed by a so-called delegate representing a Japanese company, and offering to get Japanese labourers to do farming work in western Canada?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I was interviewed by a
representative of some company that was to be organized and incorporated if the Government viewed its proposals with favour. He did not in any capacity represent the Japanese Government, who were entirely unaware of his mission. The Japanese Consul here, to whom I referred the gentleman before giving the matter further consideration, did not, I think, view the proposal with favour.

Has the minister knowledge of an effort at Belgian colonization be-
tween Smoky river and Sturgeon lake in the Peace river country?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: A Belgian priest waited on me some time ago, suggesting that he should be permitted to go to Belgium, bring some Belgians to this country and locate them on land's in Northern Alberta. I informed him that communications which we had received from the Belgian Government indicated their antagonism to the carrying on of any propoganda of that character. I did not, therefore, encourage the proposal any further.

According to the
Canada Year 'Book, there came from the United Kingdom, during the period from 1912 to 1916, a total of 483,225 people; from the United States, 476,965, and from other countries, 374,683. Adding to these figures those which the minister gave this afternoon as to the number of persons who came in during the last year, the approximate total for the five years and a half would be 491,000 from Great Britain and 916,658 from the United States and other countries. This disparity between the immigration from Great Britain and that from the United States and other countries is interesting, having in mind the suggestions made without due deliberation by some hon. gentleman with reference to the method of dealing with people who have come to Canada in large numbers in recent years, under the
10 p.m. tutelage and direction of this Government. I mention that simply because it is well that the figures should go on Hansard for future reference. I wish to ask the minister whether there is any truth in the rumour that a large settlement scheme is being arranged in Great Britain by certain well-known men who are said to be working in conjunction with this Government, undeT which certain lands in the Northwest are to be purchased and dealt with on a settlement basis.
